name: Aira Force
Wikipedia Extract: Aira Force is a waterfall in the English Lake District, in the civil parish of Matterdale and the county of Cumbria. The site of the waterfall is owned by the National Trust.
why_interesting: A spectacular 65-foot waterfall in the Lake District, framed by an arched packhorse bridge.

name: Cauldron Snout
Wikipedia Extract: Cauldron Snout is a cascade on the upper reaches of the River Tees in Northern England, immediately below the dam of the Cow Green Reservoir. It is well upstream of the High Force waterfall, and is on the boundary between County Durham and Cumbria (historically Westmorland), England.
why_interesting: One of England's longest cascades, tumbling wildly down the remote upper Tees.

name: East Gill Force
Wikipedia Extract: East Gill Force is a waterfall in Swaledale, 330 yards (300 m) east of the hamlet of Keld, in the Yorkshire Dales National Park, North Yorkshire, England. The falls are located on East Gill at grid reference NY896012,  just before its confluence with the River Swale at the point where the Pennine Way and the Coast to Coast Walk intersect.
why_interesting: A spectacular waterfall in Yorkshire Dales National Park, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Scale Force
Wikipedia Extract: Scale Force is considered the highest waterfall in the English Lake District. Opinions vary about how its precise height is calculated, but the total height is normally stated as 170 feet (51.8m).
why_interesting: The Lake District's highest single-drop waterfall, reached by a quiet fellside walk.

name: Scaleber Force
Wikipedia Extract: Scaleber Force (also known as Scaleber Foss and Scaleber Waterfall), is a 40-foot (12 m) high waterfall on Stockdale Beck, later the Long Preston Beck, that feeds into the River Ribble between Settle and Long Preston in North Yorkshire, England. The waterfall is the result of geological faulting (part of the South Craven Fault) and is a popular tourist attraction.
why_interesting: A 12-metre waterfall in North Yorkshire, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Stainforth Force
Wikipedia Extract: Stainforth Force (also known as Stainforth Foss and Ribble Falls), is a 2.5-metre (8 ft 2 in) high cascade waterfall on the River Ribble at Stainforth, 3 miles (5 km) north of Settle in North Yorkshire, England. The waterfall is a popular tourist attraction in autumn when Atlantic salmon are migrating up the river.
why_interesting: A 8-foot waterfall in North Yorkshire, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Taylor Gill Force
Wikipedia Extract: Taylor Gill Force is one of the highest waterfalls in the Lake District of England. It is situated in Seathwaite, Allerdale, near Seatoller in Cumbria.
why_interesting: Cumbria's highest waterfall, reached on a rewarding walk.

name: Wain Wath Force
Wikipedia Extract: Wain Wath Force is a waterfall on the River Swale in the Yorkshire Dales National Park, North Yorkshire, England. The falls are at grid reference NY883015, 0.6 miles (1 km) upstream from the hamlet of Keld which has three other waterfalls in its vicinity (Kisdon Force, East Gill Force, and Catrake Force).
why_interesting: A scenic stream through the countryside, perfect for a quieter wander.

name: Ingleton Waterfalls Trail
Wikipedia Extract: Ingleton Waterfalls Trail is a well-known circular trail beginning and ending in the village of Ingleton in the English county of North Yorkshire, now maintained by the Ingleton Scenery Company.  It is claimed that the trail, some 8 kilometres (5 mi) long, and with a vertical rise of 169 m (554 feet) has some of the most spectacular waterfall and woodland scenery in the north of England.
why_interesting: A famous circular walk linking a string of dramatic Yorkshire Dales waterfalls.

name: Stock Ghyll
Wikipedia Extract: Stock Ghyll, also known as Stock Gill, Stock Gill Beck and Stock Beck, is a stream in the district of Westmorland and Furness, in the ceremonial county of Cumbria and the historic county of Westmorland.  It flows about four miles from Red Screes through the town of Ambleside to the River Rothay.
why_interesting: A scenic stream through the countryside, perfect for a quieter wander.

name: Assaroe Falls
Wikipedia Extract: Assaroe Falls (Irish: Eas Aoidh Ruadh, English: the waterfall of Red Hugh), also known as Cathaleen’s Falls, was a waterfall on the River Erne near Ballyshannon, County Donegal, Ireland. It was named after Aodh Ruadh, who according to tradition, slipped and fell from the waterfall and drowned.
why_interesting: A spectacular waterfall in Ballyshannon, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Ess na Larach
Wikipedia Extract: Ess na Larach is a waterfall in Glenariff Forest Park, County Antrim, Northern Ireland. It lies along Glenariff River.
why_interesting: A spectacular waterfall in Glenariff Forest Park, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Glenmacnass Waterfall
Wikipedia Extract: Glenmacnass Waterfall (Irish: Gleann Log an Easa, meaning 'The glen of the hollow of the waterfall') is an 80-metre high waterfall situated at the head of the Glenmacnass Valley in the Wicklow Mountains in Ireland.  The Glenmacnass Waterfall is a popular tourist destination and scenic viewpoint area in the Wicklow Mountains.
why_interesting: A spectacular waterfall in Wicklow Mountains, made for walkers and photographers.

name: Kilfane
Wikipedia Extract: Kilfane (Irish: Cill Pháin) is a combination of two townlands located outside of Thomastown in County Kilkenny, Ireland. It is made up of the townlands of Kilfane East and West with a total area of 75 acres (0.30 km2).
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in County Kilkenny with a real wow factor.

name: Mullinhassig Wood
Wikipedia Extract: Mullinhassig Wood is a Coillte-owned property, straddling the townlands of Aghavrin and Shanavagha, 4 km (2.5 mi) north-west of Coachford village in County Cork, Ireland. Poulanassig Waterfall is located within the wood, 0.75 km (0.47 mi) west of the entrance, and can be viewed from the water's edge, or from a path above.
why_interesting: A wooded spot with a hidden waterfall tucked away inside.

name: Powerscourt Waterfall
Wikipedia Extract:
Powerscourt Waterfall (Irish: Eas Chonaill) is the second highest waterfall in Ireland at 121 metres (397 ft) high, it is located at the base of Glensoulan on the River Dargle near Enniskerry, County Wicklow. 
Powerscourt is overlooked by the peaks of Djouce (725 metres (2,379 ft)) and Maulin (570 metres (1,870 ft)), and flows continuously all year in a horsetail-fan pattern.
why_interesting: Ireland's second-highest waterfall, tumbling through the grounds of a grand estate.

name: River Mahon
Wikipedia Extract: The River Mahon (Irish: an Mhachain) rises in the Comeragh Mountains and enters the sea at Bunmahon in County Waterford, Ireland.
why_interesting: A river that rises in the Comeragh Mountains and reaches the sea at Bunmahon in County Waterford.

name: Toormakeady
Wikipedia Extract: Toormakeady or Tourmakeady (Irish: Tuar Mhic Éadaigh, the official name) is a Gaeltacht in south County Mayo in the west of Ireland. It is located between the shores of Lough Mask and the Partry Mountains, and covers 172.26 square kilometres (66.51 sq mi).
why_interesting: A scenic Gaeltacht between Lough Mask and the Partry Mountains.

name: Torc Waterfall
Wikipedia Extract: Torc Waterfall (from Irish Easach Toirc, meaning 'cascade of the wild boar') is a 20 metres (66 ft) high, 110 metres (360 ft) long cascade waterfall formed by the Owengarriff River as it drains from the Devil's Punchbowl corrie lake at Mangerton Mountain.  The waterfall, which lies at the base of Torc Mountain, in the Killarney National Park, is 4.3 miles (7 kilometres) from Killarney in County Kerry, Ireland.
why_interesting: A striking waterfall in Killarney National Park, an easy walk from the main road.

name: Glendalough
Wikipedia Extract: Glendalough (; Irish: Gleann Dá Loch, meaning 'valley of two lakes') is a glacial valley in County Wicklow, Ireland, renowned for an Early Medieval monastic settlement founded in the 6th century by St Kevin. From 1825 to 1957, the head of the Glendalough Valley was the site of a galena lead mine.
why_interesting: A glacial valley with two lakes and an early monastic settlement, one of Ireland's most beautiful sites.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, family, couples

name: Cairngorms National Park
Wikipedia Extract: Cairngorms National Park (Scottish Gaelic: Pàirc Nàiseanta a' Mhonaidh Ruaidh) is a national park in northeast Scotland, established in 2003. It was the second of two national parks established by the Scottish Parliament, after Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park, which was set up in 2002.
why_interesting: Britain's largest national park, home to ancient forest, arctic tundra, and ospreys.

name: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
Wikipedia Extract: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park (Scottish Gaelic: Pàirc Nàiseanta Loch Laomainn is nan Tròisichean) is a national park in Scotland centred on Loch Lomond and the hills and glens of the Trossachs, along with several other ranges of hills. It was the first of the two national parks established by the Scottish Parliament in 2002, the second being the Cairngorms National Park.
why_interesting: Scotland's first national park, centred on its largest loch and forested hills.

name: Bempton Cliffs
Wikipedia Extract: Bempton Cliffs is a section of precipitous coast at Bempton in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England. It is run by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) as a nature reserve and is known for its breeding seabirds, including northern gannet, Atlantic puffin, razorbill, common guillemot, black-legged kittiwake and fulmar.
why_interesting: Dramatic chalk cliffs alive with hundreds of thousands of nesting seabirds, including puffins.

name: Bridgwater Bay
Wikipedia Extract: Bridgwater Bay is on the Bristol Channel, 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) north of Bridgwater in Somerset, England at the mouth of the River Parrett and the end of the River Parrett Trail. It stretches from Minehead at the southwestern end of the bay to Brean Down in the north.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in Somerset, made for a memorable day out.
Good For: family, couples, walkers and hikers, photographers, day trip

name: Fairburn Ings RSPB reserve
Wikipedia Extract:
Fairburn Ings Nature Reserve is a protected area in West Yorkshire, England, noted for its avian biodiversity.
The reserve has recorded around 280 bird species, remarkable for an inland site in the United Kingdom.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in West Yorkshire with a real wow factor.

name: Foulney Island
Wikipedia Extract: Foulney Island is a low-lying grass and shingle area 1 mile (1.6 km) to the south-east of Roa Island, off the southern tip of the Furness Peninsula in Cumbria, England. Foulney Island is one of the Islands of Furness in Morecambe Bay, northern England.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in Cumbria, made for a memorable day out.
Good For: family, couples, walkers and hikers, photographers, day trip

name: Aldbury Nowers
Wikipedia Extract: Aldbury Nowers is a 19.7 hectares (49 acres) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) in the Chiltern Hills, north-east of Tring in Hertfordshire. The site was notified in 1990 under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Hertfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Brownsea Island
Wikipedia Extract: Brownsea Island is the largest of the islands in Poole Harbour, in the county of Dorset, England. The island is owned by the National Trust, with the northern half managed by the Dorset Wildlife Trust.
why_interesting: A National Trust island sanctuary for red squirrels, reached by boat across Poole Harbour.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Cassiobury Park
Wikipedia Extract: Cassiobury Park is the principal public park in Watford, Hertfordshire, in England. It was created in 1909 from the purchase by Watford Borough Council of part of the estate of the Earls of Essex around Cassiobury House which was subsequently demolished in 1927.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in England with a real wow factor.

name: Ant Broads & Marshes National Nature Reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Ant Broads & Marshes NNR is a national nature reserve in Norfolk, England established by English Nature. It is named after the River Ant.
why_interesting: A scenic river in Norfolk, shaped by some lovely countryside.

name: Arne RSPB reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Arne RSPB reserve is a 5.634-square-kilometre (1,392-acre) nature reserve and Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) maintained by the RSPB and located in Dorset. It was notified as an SSSI in 1986 and the estuarine reedbeds within the site are designated as a national nature reserve.
why_interesting: A lowland heath reserve on Poole Harbour, one of the best places in Britain to see rare Dartford warblers.

name: Aston Rowant National Nature Reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Aston Rowant National Nature Reserve is located on the north-west escarpment of the Chiltern Hills, in the Chilterns Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It has an area of 159.1 hectares (393 acres), and most of it is a 128.5 hectares (318 acres) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in north-west escarpment of the Chiltern Hills with a real wow factor.

name: Ballard Down
Wikipedia Extract: Ballard Down is an area of chalk downland on the Purbeck Hills in the English county of Dorset. The hills meet the English Channel here, and Ballard Down forms a headland, Ballard Point, between Studland Bay to the north and Swanage Bay to the south.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in English county of Dorset, made for a memorable day out.
Good For: family, couples, walkers and hikers, photographers, day trip

name: Bassenthwaite Lake
Wikipedia Extract: Bassenthwaite Lake is a body of water in the Lake District in North West England, near the town of Keswick. It has an area of 5.3 km2 (2.0 sq mi), making the fourth largest of the lakes in the region.
why_interesting: The only body of water in the Lake District still officially called a 'lake', home to breeding ospreys.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, family, couples

name: Benacre National Nature Reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Benacre National Nature Reserve is a national nature reserve in the English county of Suffolk. It is located on the North Sea coast in the parishes of Benacre, Covehithe, Reydon and South Cove.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in parishes of Benacre, made for a memorable day out.

name: Bure Marshes National Nature Reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Bure Marshes National Nature Reserve is a national nature reserve (NNR) in Norfolk, England. Created in 1958, the reserve covers 451.5 hectares of wetland within the floodplain of the River Bure.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in Norfolk, made for a memorable day out.

name: Burnham Beeches
Wikipedia Extract: Burnham Beeches is a 374.6-hectare (926-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest situated west of Farnham Common in the village of Burnham, Buckinghamshire. The southern half is owned by the Corporation of London and is open to the public.
why_interesting: Ancient pollarded beech woodland on London's doorstep, some trees over 400 years old.

name: Calthorpe Broad
Wikipedia Extract: Calthorpe Broad is a 43.5-hectare (107-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest east of Stalham in Norfolk, England. It is a Nature Conservation Review site, Grade I and a national nature reserve.
why_interesting: A scenic viewpoint with sweeping Norfolk views.

name: Hambledon Hill
Wikipedia Extract: Hambledon Hill is a prehistoric hill fort in Dorset, England, in the Blackmore Vale five miles northwest of Blandford Forum. The hill itself is a chalk outcrop, on the southwestern corner of Cranborne Chase, separated from the Dorset Downs by the River Stour.
why_interesting: A dramatic Iron Age hillfort with sweeping views across the Dorset countryside.

name: Hickling Broad
Wikipedia Extract: Hickling Broad is a  600-hectare (1,500-acre) nature reserve 4 km south-east of Stalham, north-east of Norwich in Norfolk. It is managed by the Norfolk Wildlife Trust.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Norfolk with a real wow factor.

name: Holkham National Nature Reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Holkham National Nature Reserve is one of England's largest national nature reserve (NNR). It is on the Norfolk coast between Burnham Overy Staithe and Blakeney, and is managed by Natural England with the cooperation of the Holkham Estate.
why_interesting: One of England's largest nature reserves, with vast pine-backed dunes and beach.

name: Hutton Roof Crags
Wikipedia Extract: Hutton Roof Crags is a hill in southeastern Cumbria in northwest England, located near to the village of Hutton Roof. It has extensive areas of limestone pavement as well as grassland and woodland.
why_interesting: A limestone pavement hill in Cumbria, rich in rare plants and dramatic karst scenery.
Good For: walkers and hikers, family, solo travelling

name: Ingleborough
Wikipedia Extract: Ingleborough (723 m or 2,372 ft) is the second-highest mountain in the Yorkshire Dales, England. It is one of the Yorkshire Three Peaks (the other two being Whernside and Pen-y-ghent), and is frequently climbed as part of the Three Peaks walk.
why_interesting: One of the Yorkshire Three Peaks, its flat summit ringed by an Iron Age hillfort.

name: Kinder Scout
Wikipedia Extract: Kinder Scout is a moorland plateau and National Nature Reserve in the Dark Peak of the Derbyshire Peak District in England. Part of the moor, at 636 metres (2,087 ft) above sea level, is the highest point in the Peak District, in Derbyshire and the East Midlands.
why_interesting: The Peak District's highest point, site of the famous 1932 mass trespass for the right to roam.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Berney Marshes & Breydon Water RSPB reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Berney Marshes and Breydon Water RSPB reserve is a nature reserve managed by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB). Berney Marshes is situated south of the River Bure while Breydon water is the combined estuary of the River Waveney and the River Yare inland from Great Yarmouth in Norfolk, England.
why_interesting: A scenic river in Norfolk, shaped by some lovely countryside.

name: Breydon Water
Wikipedia Extract: Breydon Water is a 514.4-hectare (1,271-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest at Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, England. It is a Local Nature Reserve, a Ramsar site and a Special Protection Area.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Great Yarmouth with a real wow factor.

name: Coombes Valley RSPB reserve
Wikipedia Extract: Coombes Valley RSPB reserve (grid reference SK005525) is a nature reserve, run by the RSPB, near the town of Leek in Staffordshire, England. It is best known for its breeding woodland birds, including common redstart, wood warbler and pied flycatcher.
why_interesting: A gorgeous woodland escape in Staffordshire with a wonderfully wild feel.
Good For: walkers and hikers, family, solo travelling

name: Coquet Island
Wikipedia Extract: Coquet Island  is a small island of about 6 hectares (15 acres), situated 1.2 kilometres (0.75 mi) off Amble on the Northumberland coast, northeast England. It is included in the civil parish of Hauxley.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in Northumberland coast, made for a memorable day out.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Spurn
Wikipedia Extract: Spurn is a narrow sand tidal island located off the tip of the coast of the East Riding of Yorkshire, England that reaches into the North Sea and forms the north bank of the mouth of the Humber Estuary. It was a spit with a semi-permanent connection to the mainland, but a storm in 2013 made the road down to the end of Spurn impassable to vehicles at high tide.
why_interesting: A dramatic, ever-shifting sand spit reaching out into the Humber estuary.

name: Ouse Washes
Wikipedia Extract: Ouse Washes is a linear 2,513.6-hectare (6,211-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest stretching from near St Ives in Cambridgeshire to Downham Market in Norfolk, England. It is also a Ramsar internationally important wetland site, a Special Protection Area for birds, a Special Area of Conservation and a Nature Conservation Review site, Grade I. An area of 186 hectares (460 acres) between March and Ely is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire and another area near Chatteris is managed by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds.
why_interesting: A scenic viewpoint with sweeping Cambridgeshire to Downham Market in Norfolk views.

name: Cooper's Hill, Bedfordshire
Wikipedia Extract: Cooper's Hill is an 18.1-hectare (45-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest in Ampthill in Bedfordshire. It was notified under Section 28  of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in 1984, and the planning authority is Central Bedfordshire Council.
why_interesting: A pub with literary connections and plenty of atmosphere.

name: Cople Pits
Wikipedia Extract: Cople Pits is a 2-hectare (4.9-acre) nature reserve in Cople in Bedfordshire. It is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Cople in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Cut-throat Meadow
Wikipedia Extract: Cut-throat Meadow is a 1.5 hectare nature reserve in Ampthill in Bedfordshire. It is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Ampthill in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Dropshort Marsh
Wikipedia Extract: Dropshort Marsh is a 2.7-hectare (6.7-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest in Toddington in Bedfordshire. It was notified under Section 28 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in 1985, and the local planning authority is Central Bedfordshire Council.
why_interesting: A pub with literary connections and plenty of atmosphere.

name: Felmersham Gravel Pits
Wikipedia Extract: Felmersham Gravel Pits is a 21.6-hectare (53-acre) Site of Special Scientific Interest between the villages of Felmersham and Sharnbrook in Bedfordshire. It was notified under Section 28 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in 1986 and the local planning authority is Bedford Borough Council.
why_interesting: A pub with literary connections and plenty of atmosphere.

name: Flitwick Moor
Wikipedia Extract: Flitwick Moor is a 59.8-hectare (148-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest between Flitwick and Greenfield in Bedfordshire. It was notified under Section 28 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in 1984 and the local planning authority is Central Bedfordshire Council.
why_interesting: A pub with literary connections and plenty of atmosphere.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Castle Archdale
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Archdale in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, is a former estate on the shores of Lough Erne Lower, the key feature of which today is Castle Archdale Country Park. There is also a caravan park.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in shores of Lough Erne Lower, made for a memorable day out.

name: Crom Estate
Wikipedia Extract: The Crom Estate (, Irish: An Chrom) is a nature reserve located in the south-east of County Fermanagh in Northern Ireland, along the shores of Upper Lough Erne. It is one of three estates owned and managed by the National Trust in County Fermanagh, the others being Florence Court and Castle Coole.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot made for a memorable day out.

name: Giant's Causeway
Wikipedia Extract: The Giant's Causeway (Irish: Clochán an Aifir or Clochán na bhFomhórach) is an area of approximately 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, the result of an ancient volcanic fissure eruption, part of the North Atlantic Igneous Province active in the region during the Paleogene period. It is located in County Antrim on the north coast of Northern Ireland, about three miles (4.8 km) northeast of the town of Bushmills.
why_interesting: Thousands of interlocking hexagonal basalt columns, formed by an ancient volcanic eruption.

name: Lough Beg
Wikipedia Extract: Lough Beg (from Irish  Loch Beag 'little lake') is a small freshwater lake north of Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland. The lake is located on the border between County Londonderry and County Antrim.
why_interesting: A beautiful waterside spot in Northern Ireland with a real sense of calm and space.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, family, couples

name: Pavenham Osier Beds
Wikipedia Extract: Pavenham Osier Beds is a 1.3 hectare nature reserve south of Pavenham, on the banks of the River Great Ouse, in Bedfordshire. It is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A scenic river in Bedfordshire, shaped by some lovely countryside.

name: Pegsdon Hills and Hoo Bit
Wikipedia Extract: Pegsdon Hills and Hoo Bit is a 79-hectare (200-acre) nature reserve in Pegsdon in Bedfordshire. It is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Pegsdon in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Sallowsprings
Wikipedia Extract: Sallowsprings is a 1.3-hectare (3.2-acre) nature reserve in Whipsnade in Bedfordshire. It is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Whipsnade in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Sewell Cutting
Wikipedia Extract: Sewell Cutting is a 3.6-hectare (8.9-acre) nature reserve at Sewell in Houghton Regis in Bedfordshire. It is owned by Central Bedfordshire Council and managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Houghton Regis in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Sharnbrook Summit
Wikipedia Extract: Sharnbrook Summit is a nature reserve between the villages of Sharnbrook and Wymington in Bedfordshire. It has an area of approximately nine hectares, and it is managed by the Wildlife Trust for Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Northamptonshire.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in Bedfordshire with a real wow factor.

name: Castle Espie
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Espie is a wetland reserve managed by the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) on the banks of Strangford Lough, three miles south of Comber, County Down, Northern Ireland, in the townland of the same name. It is part of the Strangford Lough Ramsar Site.
why_interesting: A striking natural landscape in banks of Strangford Lough with a real wow factor.

name: Eigg
Wikipedia Extract: Eigg ( EG; Scottish Gaelic: Eige [ˈekʲə] ) is one of the Small Isles in the Scottish Inner Hebrides. It lies to the south of the island of Skye and to the north of the Ardnamurchan peninsula.
why_interesting: A small, community-owned Hebridean island beneath the dramatic volcanic ridge of An Sgurr.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Fair Isle
Wikipedia Extract: Fair Isle (Shaetlan pronunciation: [ˌfɛər ˈaɪl]  fair EYEL; Old Norse: Friðarey) is the southernmost of the Shetland Islands, Scotland. It is situated at the approximate midpoint between the southern tip of Mainland, Shetland; and North Ronaldsay, the northernmost of the Orkney Islands; in an area bordering the North Sea and the Atlantic Ocean known as the Fair Isle Gap.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most remote inhabited islands, famed for its birdlife and traditional knitwear.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Glen Finglas Estate
Wikipedia Extract: The Glen Finglas Estate is a property in Glen Finglas in the Trossachs, Scotland managed by The Woodland Trust. The estate extends for over 10,000 acres (4,000 ha), most of which was once covered in woodland.
why_interesting: A beautiful coastal spot in woodland, made for a memorable day out.
Good For: walkers and hikers, family, solo travelling

name: Abernethy Forest
Wikipedia Extract: Abernethy Forest is a remnant of the Caledonian Forest in Strathspey, in the Highland council area of Scotland. It lies within the Cairngorms National Park, close to the villages of Nethy Bridge, Boat of Garten, and Aviemore.
why_interesting: A gorgeous woodland escape in Highland council area of Scotland with a wonderfully wild feel.
Good For: walkers and hikers, family, solo travelling

name: Beinn Eighe
Wikipedia Extract: Beinn Eighe (Scottish Gaelic for 'file mountain') is a mountain massif in the Torridon area of Wester Ross in the Northwest Highlands of Scotland. Lying south of Loch Maree, it forms a long ridge with many spurs and summits, two of which are classified as Munros: Ruadh-stac Mòr at 1,010 m (3,314 ft) and Spidean Coire nan Clach at 993 m (3,258 ft).
why_interesting: Britain's oldest National Nature Reserve, a dramatic quartzite mountain in Wester Ross.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Ben Lawers
Wikipedia Extract: Ben Lawers (Scottish Gaelic: Beinn Labhair) is the highest mountain in the Breadalbane region of the Scottish Highlands. It lies north of Loch Tay and is the highest peak of the 'Ben Lawers group', a ridge that includes six other Munros: Beinn Ghlas, Meall Garbh, Meall Corranaich, An Stùc, Meall Greigh and Meall a' Choire Leith.
why_interesting: The highest mountain in the southern Highlands, renowned for its rare alpine flowers.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Ben Wyvis
Wikipedia Extract: Ben Wyvis (Scottish Gaelic: Beinn Uais) is a mountain in Easter Ross, in the northern Highlands of Scotland. It lies north-west of Dingwall, in the council area of Highland, and the county of Ross and Cromarty.
why_interesting: A distinctive whale-backed mountain rising above the northern Highlands.
Good For: walkers and hikers, photographers, solo travelling

name: Corstorphine Hill
Wikipedia Extract: Corstorphine Hill is a low ridge-shaped hill rising above the western suburbs of Edinburgh, Scotland. Although there has been residential and commercial development on its lower slopes, especially in the south and west, most of the hill is occupied by a local nature reserve, consisting of extensive broadleaf woodland, accessible to the public.
why_interesting: A gorgeous woodland escape in south with a wonderfully wild feel.
Good For: walkers and hikers, family, solo travelling

name: Dawsholm Park
Wikipedia Extract: Dawsholm Park is a public park in Glasgow, Scotland, adjoining the Kelvindale, Maryhill and Temple areas of the city, and southern parts of the town of Bearsden. It is situated on the River Kelvin, north of the River Clyde.

name: Foula

name: Digswell Viaduct

name: Kew Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Kew Bridge  is a wide-span bridge over the Tideway (upper estuary of the Thames) linking the London Boroughs of Richmond upon Thames and Hounslow. The present bridge, which was opened in 1903 as King Edward VII Bridge by King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra, was designed by John Wolfe-Barry and Cuthbert Arthur Brereton.
why_interesting: A handsome stone bridge crossing the Thames beside Kew Gardens.

name: Kew Railway Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Kew Railway Bridge spans the River Thames in London, England, between Kew and Strand-on-the-Green, Chiswick. The bridge was opened in 1869.
why_interesting: A distinctive lattice railway bridge crossing the River Thames at Kew.

name: Lambeth Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Lambeth Bridge is a road traffic and footbridge crossing the River Thames in an east–west direction in central London. The river flows north at the crossing point.
why_interesting: The red-painted bridge linking Westminster with Lambeth Palace.

name: Putney Bridge
Wikipedia Extract:
Putney Bridge is a Grade II listed bridge over the River Thames in west London, linking Putney on the south side with Fulham to the north. 
Before the first bridge on the site, known as Fulham Bridge, was built in 1729, a ferry had shuttled between the two banks.
why_interesting: London's oldest surviving bridge across the Thames in its original location.

name: Southwark Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Southwark Bridge (  SUDH-ərk) is an arch bridge in London, for traffic linking the district of Southwark and the City across the River Thames. Besides when others are closed for temporary repairs, it has the least traffic of the Thames bridges in London.
why_interesting: A graceful steel arch bridge connecting the City with Southwark.

name: Teddington Lock Footbridges
Wikipedia Extract: The Teddington Lock Footbridges are two footbridges over the River Thames in England, situated just upstream of Teddington Lock at Teddington. There is a small island between the bridges.
why_interesting: Elegant Victorian footbridges crossing Teddington Lock and the River Thames.

name: Brig o' Balgownie
Wikipedia Extract: The Brig o' Balgownie is a 13th-century bridge spanning the River Don in Old Aberdeen, Scotland. It is the oldest standing bridge in Scotland.
why_interesting: Scotland's oldest surviving bridge, spanning the River Don since the 13th century.

name: Craigellachie Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Craigellachie Bridge is a cast iron arch bridge across the River Spey at Craigellachie, near to the village of Aberlour in Moray, Scotland. It was designed by the renowned civil engineer Thomas Telford and built from 1812 to 1814.
why_interesting: Thomas Telford's elegant cast-iron bridge crossing the River Spey.

name: Brig o' Doon
Wikipedia Extract: The Brig o' Doon (or Brig O'Doon), sometimes called the Auld Brig or Old Bridge of Doon, is a late medieval bridge over the River Doon in Ayrshire, Scotland, and a Category A listed historic structure.
why_interesting: The beautiful medieval bridge immortalised in Robert Burns' poetry.

name: Eglinton Tournament Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Eglinton Tournament Bridge is a bridge located within Eglinton Country Park near Kilwinning, North Ayrshire, Scotland. The bridge crosses the Lugton Water a short distance northwest of Eglinton Castle (grid reference NS 3206 4224) and was named after the Eglinton Tournament of 1839.
why_interesting: A picturesque Gothic bridge built for Scotland's famous Eglinton Tournament.

name: Conwy Suspension Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Conwy Suspension Bridge is a Grade I-listed structure and is one of the first road suspension bridges in the world. Located in the medieval town of Conwy in Conwy county borough, North Wales, it is now only passable on foot.
why_interesting: Thomas Telford's elegant suspension bridge beside Conwy Castle.

name: Ha'penny Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The  Ha'penny Bridge ( HAYP-nee; Irish: Droichead na Leathphingine, or Droichead na Life), known later for a time as the Penny Ha'penny Bridge, and officially the Liffey Bridge, is a pedestrian bridge built in May 1816 over the River Liffey in Dublin, Ireland. Made of cast iron, the bridge was cast in Shropshire, England.
why_interesting: Dublin's iconic white pedestrian bridge crossing the River Liffey.

name: East-Link (Dublin)
Wikipedia Extract: The Tom Clarke Bridge (Irish: Droichead Thomáis Uí Chléirigh), formerly and commonly known as the East-Link Toll Bridge, is a toll bridge in Dublin, Ireland, on the River Liffey, owned and operated by Dublin City Council. The bascule-type lifting bridge, which links North Wall to Ringsend, is the last bridge on the Liffey, which opens out into Dublin Port and then Dublin Bay just beyond.
why_interesting: The modern toll bridge spanning Dublin Port and the River Liffey.

name: Baconsthorpe Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Baconsthorpe Castle, historically known as Baconsthorpe Hall, is a ruined, fortified manor house near the village of Baconsthorpe, Norfolk, England. It was established in the 15th century on the site of a former manor hall, probably by John Heydon I and his father, William.
why_interesting: The picturesque ruins of a moated Norman castle hidden in the Norfolk countryside.

name: Bolingbroke Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bolingbroke Castle is a ruined castle in Bolingbroke (now Old Bolingbroke) in Lincolnshire, England.
why_interesting: The romantic ruins of the birthplace of Henry IV in rural Lincolnshire.

name: Bolsover Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bolsover Castle is in the town of Bolsover (grid reference SK471707), in the north-east of the English county of Derbyshire. Built in the early 17th century, the present castle lies on the earthworks and ruins of the 12th-century medieval castle; the first structure of the present castle was built between 1612 and 1617 by Sir Charles Cavendish.
why_interesting: A spectacular Stuart mansion blending palace and fortress above the Derbyshire countryside.

name: Cambridge Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Cambridge Castle, locally also known as Castle Mound, is in Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, England. Built after the Norman Conquest of England in 1066 to control the strategically important route to the north of England, it played a role in the conflicts of the Anarchy and the First and Second Barons' Wars.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of Cambridge's Norman motte-and-bailey castle.

name: Clun Castle
why_interesting: The dramatic riverside ruins of one of the Welsh Marches' greatest castles.

name: Conisbrough Castle
why_interesting: One of England's finest Norman keeps, offering spectacular views across South Yorkshire.

name: Edlingham Castle
why_interesting: A unique fortified manor house surrounded by a medieval moat in Northumberland.

name: Kenilworth Castle
why_interesting: One of England's greatest castle ruins, famed for Elizabeth I's visit to Robert Dudley.

name: Beacon Hill Battery
Wikipedia Extract: Beacon Hill Battery (also known as Beacon Hill Fort) is a late-19th and 20th century coastal fortification that was built to defend the port of Harwich, Essex. It is a scheduled ancient monument.
why_interesting: A Second World War coastal battery overlooking the Firth of Clyde.

name: Calshot Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Calshot Castle is an artillery fort constructed by Henry VIII on the Calshot Spit, Hampshire, England, between 1539 and 1540. It formed part of the King's Device programme to protect against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire and defend Southampton Water as it met the Solent.
why_interesting: One of Henry VIII's finest artillery forts guarding Southampton Water.

name: Camber Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Camber Castle, also known formerly as Winchelsea Castle, is a 16th-century Device Fort, built near Rye by King Henry VIII to protect the Sussex coast of England against French attack. The first fortification on the site was a small, round artillery tower, constructed by Henry between 1512 and 1514, overlooking the Camber anchorage and the entrance to Rye Harbour.
why_interesting: A rare concentric artillery fort standing alone in the Romney Marshes.

name: Deal Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Deal Castle is an artillery fort constructed by Henry VIII in Deal, Kent, between 1539 and 1540. It formed part of the King's Device programme to protect against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire, and defended the strategically important Downs anchorage off the English coast.
why_interesting: Henry VIII's best-preserved artillery fort, built to defend the Downs.

name: Middleham Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Middleham Castle is a ruined castle in Middleham in Wensleydale, in the county of North Yorkshire, England. It was built by Robert Fitzrandolph, 3rd Lord of Middleham and Spennithorne, commencing in 1190.
why_interesting: The mighty childhood home of Richard III overlooking Wensleydale.

name: Newark Castle, Nottinghamshire
Wikipedia Extract: Newark Castle, in Newark-on-Trent in the English county of Nottinghamshire, was founded in the mid 12th century by Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln. Originally a timber castle, it was rebuilt in stone towards the end of the century.
why_interesting: The impressive riverside ruins of a Norman castle in the heart of Newark.

name: Sandsfoot Castle
why_interesting: The romantic cliff-top ruins overlooking Weymouth Bay.

name: Sherborne Castle
why_interesting: A magnificent stately home surrounded by a landscaped Capability Brown park.

name: Pontefract Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Pontefract (or Pomfret) Castle is a castle ruin in the town of Pontefract, in West Yorkshire, England. King Richard II is thought to have died there.
why_interesting: The dramatic ruins of one of England's most important royal castles.

name: Hurst Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Hurst Castle is an artillery fort established by Henry VIII on the Hurst Spit in Hampshire, England, between 1541 and 1544. It formed part of the king's Device Forts coastal protection programme against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire, and defended the western entrance to the Solent waterway.
why_interesting: One of Henry VIII's greatest coastal forts, guarding the western Solent.

name: Walmer Castle
why_interesting: A Tudor coastal fortress that later became the Duke of Wellington's residence.

name: Yarmouth Castle
why_interesting: Henry VIII's compact coastal fortress overlooking the western Solent.

name: Carisbrooke Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Carisbrooke Castle is a historic motte-and-bailey castle located above, and to the south of, Carisbrooke village centre, on the Isle of Wight, England. Charles I was imprisoned at the castle in the months prior to his trial.
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved medieval castles, once the prison of Charles I.

name: Carlisle Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Carlisle Castle is a stone keep medieval fortress located in the city of Carlisle near the ruins of Hadrian's Wall. First built during the reign of William II in 1092 and rebuilt in stone under Henry I in 1122, the castle is over 930 years old and has been the scene of many episodes in British history.
why_interesting: A mighty border fortress that has defended Carlisle for over 900 years.

name: Lancaster Castle
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved castles, combining medieval history with a working courthouse.

name: Tynemouth Priory and Castle
why_interesting: A spectacular clifftop priory and castle overlooking the North Sea.

name: Bedford Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bedford Castle was a large medieval castle in Bedford, England. Built after 1100 by Henry I, the castle played a prominent part in both the civil war of the Anarchy and the First Barons' War.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of Bedford's Norman castle overlooking the Great Ouse.

name: Biggleswade Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Biggleswade Castle was a ringwork and bailey castle in the market town of Biggleswade in Bedfordshire, England.
The existence of this castle was discovered by aerial photography, in 1954.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a Norman motte overlooking the market town of Biggleswade.

name: Brightwell Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Brightwell Castle was in the village of Brightwell-cum-Sotwell, between the towns of Didcot and Wallingford (grid reference SU578908), now in Oxfordshire but until 1974 in Berkshire, in England.
The castle was built in 1145 by King Stephen.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a Norman motte hidden in the Oxfordshire countryside.

name: Buckingham Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Buckingham Castle was situated in the town of Buckingham, the former county town of Buckinghamshire, on the north side of the River Ouse.
The castle was first mentioned in documentary sources in 1154–64 and was possibly demolished 1208–1215.
why_interesting: The site of the Norman castle that gave Buckingham its name.

name: Cainhoe Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Cainhoe Castle was an 11th-century Norman castle, located near the village of Clophill, in the county of Bedfordshire, England.
Cainhoe Castle was a motte and triple bailey castle, built by Nigel d'Aubigny, a Norman Knight, sometime after the Norman Invasion (1066).
why_interesting: The impressive earthworks of a Norman motte-and-bailey overlooking Bedfordshire.

name: Desborough Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Desborough Castle is an Iron Age hill fort which lies on the southern side of the valley of the River Wye in Buckinghamshire, which runs through the Chiltern Hills from The Ridgeway and Vale of Aylesbury to the river Thames.
why_interesting: A well-preserved Norman motte rising above the Buckinghamshire countryside.

name: Dinton Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dinton Castle (also known as Dinton Folly) is located just north of the village of Dinton, in Buckinghamshire and was built as an eyecatcher from the Dinton Hall estate, by Sir John Vanhatten in 1769. He used the castle to exhibit his collection of fossils, ammonites, embedded in the limestone walls.
why_interesting: An unusual triangular Gothic folly built to resemble a medieval castle.

name: Donnington Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Donnington Castle is a ruined medieval castle, situated in the small village of Donnington, just north of the town of Newbury in the English county of Berkshire. It was founded by Sir Richard Abberbury the Elder in 1386 and was bought by Thomas Chaucer before the castle was taken under royal control during the Tudor period.
why_interesting: The impressive Civil War ruins of a medieval castle overlooking the Kennet Valley.

name: Windsor Castle
why_interesting: The world's oldest and largest occupied castle, home to British monarchs for nearly 1,000 years.

name: Beeston Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Beeston Castle is a former Royal castle in Beeston, Cheshire, England (grid reference SJ537593), perched on a rocky sandstone crag 350 feet (107 m) above the Cheshire Plain. It was built in the 1220s by Ranulf de Blondeville, 6th Earl of Chester (1170–1232), on his return from the Crusades.
why_interesting: A spectacular hilltop fortress with panoramic views across the Cheshire Plain.

name: Chester Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Chester Castle is in the city of Chester, Cheshire, England. It is sited at the southwest extremity of the area bounded by the city walls.
why_interesting: The imposing Norman fortress overlooking the River Dee in the heart of Chester.

name: Halton Castle
why_interesting: The dramatic hilltop ruins of a Norman castle overlooking the Mersey Estuary.

name: Bickleigh Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bickleigh Castle is a fortified manor house that stands on the banks of the River Exe at Bickleigh in Devon, England. Once considerably larger, Bickleigh now comprises a group of buildings from various periods which together formed a water castle.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved moated manor house surrounded by the River Exe.

name: Castle Drogo
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Drogo is a country house and mixed-revivalist castle near Drewsteignton, Devon, England. Constructed between 1911 and 1930, it is the last castle built in England.
why_interesting: The last castle built in England, dramatically perched above Dartmoor.

name: Compton Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Compton Castle in the parish of Marldon in Devon, is a fortified manor house in the village of Compton (formerly "Compton Pole"), about 5 miles (8 km) west of Torquay on the southern coast of Devon, England (grid reference SX865648). The estate was home to the families of Compton, de la Pole, Doddiscombe, Gilbert and Templer.
why_interesting: One of England's finest fortified manor houses, enclosed by a medieval curtain wall.

name: Duffield Castle, Derbyshire
Wikipedia Extract: Duffield Castle was a Norman castle in Duffield, Derbyshire. The site is a scheduled monument.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a mighty Norman castle overlooking the Derwent Valley.

name: Elvaston Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Elvaston Castle is a stately home in Elvaston, Derbyshire, England. The Gothic Revival castle and surrounding parkland is run and owned by Derbyshire County Council as a country park known as Elvaston Castle Country Park.
why_interesting: A romantic Gothic Revival mansion set within landscaped parkland.

name: Naworth Castle
why_interesting: A magnificent medieval fortress that has remained a family home for over 700 years.

name: Powderham Castle
why_interesting: A magnificent riverside castle overlooking the Exe Estuary for more than 600 years.

name: Auckland Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Auckland Castle, also known as Auckland Palace, is a former bishop's palace located in the town of Bishop Auckland in County Durham, England. The castle was a residence of the bishops of Durham from approximately 1183 and was their primary residence between 1832 and 2012, when the castle and its contents were sold to the Auckland Castle Trust (now the Auckland Project).
why_interesting: The historic palace of the Prince Bishops of Durham, transformed into a world-class heritage attraction.

name: Bowes Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bowes Castle is a medieval castle in the village of Bowes in County Durham, England. Built within the perimeter of the former Roman fort of Lavatrae, on the Roman road that is now the A66, the early timber castle on the site was replaced by a more substantial stone structure between 1170 and 1174 on the orders of Henry II. A planned village was built alongside the castle.
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved Norman keeps, standing dramatically above the River Greta.

name: Corfe Castle (village)
Wikipedia Extract: Corfe Castle is a village and civil parish in the English county of Dorset. It is the site of a ruined castle of the same name.
why_interesting: The iconic castle ruins towering above one of Dorset's prettiest villages.

name: Corfe Castle Hundred
Wikipedia Extract:
Corfe Castle Hundred was a hundred in the county of Dorset, England, containing only the parish of Corfe Castle.
It was sometimes also referred to as Corfe Castle Liberty.

name: Corfe Castle railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle,  in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972.
why_interesting: The heritage railway station at the foot of the iconic castle ruins.

name: Lulworth Castle
why_interesting: A magnificent 17th-century hunting lodge enclosed within towering medieval walls.

name: Bodiam Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bodiam Castle () is a 14th-century moated castle near Robertsbridge in East Sussex, England. It was built in 1385 by Sir Edward Dalyngrigge with the permission of Richard II, ostensibly to defend the area against French invasion during the Hundred Years' War.
why_interesting: One of England's most photographed moated castles, straight from a fairy tale.

name: Colchester Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Colchester Castle is a Norman castle in Colchester, Essex, England, dating from the second half of the eleventh century.  It is located in, and gives its name to, Castle Park.
why_interesting: Europe's largest Norman keep, built on the foundations of a Roman temple.

name: Lambton Castle
why_interesting: A grand Gothic Revival castle overlooking the River Wear.

name: Lewes Castle
why_interesting: A Norman stronghold offering spectacular views across the Sussex Downs.

name: Severndroog Castle
why_interesting: A striking Gothic folly overlooking Shooters Hill.

name: Basing House
Wikipedia Extract: Basing House was a Tudor palace and castle in the village of Old Basing in the English county of Hampshire. It once rivalled Hampton Court Palace in its size and opulence.
why_interesting: The vast Tudor palace-fortress that endured one of the English Civil War's greatest sieges.

name: Berkeley Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Berkeley Castle ( BARK-lee; historically sometimes spelled as Berkley Castle or Barkley Castle) is a castle in the town of Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England. The castle's origins date back to the 11th century and it is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: One of England's oldest inhabited castles, home to the Berkeley family for nearly 900 years.

name: Eastnor Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Eastnor Castle, Eastnor, Herefordshire, is a 19th-century mock castle. Eastnor was built for John Cocks, 1st Earl Somers, who employed Robert Smirke, later the main architect of the British Museum.
why_interesting: A magnificent Victorian castle overlooking the Malvern Hills.

name: Highclere Castle
why_interesting: The grand country house made famous worldwide as Downton Abbey.

name: Portchester Castle
why_interesting: One of the best-preserved Roman forts in northern Europe, enclosed within medieval walls.

name: Winchester Castle
why_interesting: The magnificent Great Hall, all that remains of Winchester's Norman castle.

name: Allington Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Allington Castle is a stone castle in Allington, Kent, just north of Maidstone, in England. The first castle on the site was an unauthorised fortification, built during "The Anarchy" (1135–1153) and torn down later in the century when royal control was reasserted.
why_interesting: A picturesque moated castle hidden in the Kent countryside.

name: Ashby de la Zouch Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Ashby de la Zouch Castle is a ruined fortification in the town of Ashby-de-la-Zouch, Leicestershire, England. The castle was built by William, Lord Hastings, a favourite of Edward IV, after 1473, accompanied by the creation of a 3,000-acre (1,200 ha) park.
why_interesting: The impressive ruins of a great Tudor palace-fortress overlooking Leicestershire.

name: Belvoir Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Belvoir Castle (  BEE-vər) is a faux historic castle and stately home in Leicestershire, England, situated 6 mi (10 km) west of the town of Grantham and 10 mi (16 km) northeast of Melton Mowbray. A castle was first built on the site immediately after the Norman Conquest of 1066 and has since been rebuilt at least three times.
why_interesting: A spectacular Gothic Revival castle dominating the Vale of Belvoir.

name: Chiddingstone Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Chiddingstone Castle is situated in the village of Chiddingstone, near Edenbridge, Kent, England, 35 miles (56 kilometres) south-southeast of London and in the upper valley of the River Medway. The castle was built by the Streatfeild family and served as their seat from the early 16th century until the beginning of the 20th century when the family left the castle.
why_interesting: A beautiful historic house filled with eclectic collections and surrounded by tranquil gardens.

name: Dover Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dover Castle is a medieval castle in Dover, Kent, England and is Grade I listed. It was founded in the 11th century and has been described as the "Key to England" due to its defensive significance throughout history.
why_interesting: England's greatest medieval fortress, guarding the White Cliffs for over 900 years.

name: Hever Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Hever Castle ( HEE-və) is located in the village of Hever, Kent, near Edenbridge, 30 miles (48 km) south-east of London, England. It began as a country house, built in the 13th century.
why_interesting: The romantic moated childhood home of Anne Boleyn.

name: Burgh Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Burgh Castle is a village and civil parish in the English county of Norfolk. It is 3 miles (4.8 km) south-west of Great Yarmouth and 16 miles (26 km) east of Norwich.
why_interesting: One of Britain's best-preserved Roman Saxon Shore forts overlooking Breydon Water.

name: Kirby Muxloe Castle
why_interesting: A rare unfinished brick castle surrounded by a picturesque moat.

name: Tower of London
why_interesting: The world's most famous medieval fortress, home to the Crown Jewels.

name: Alnwick Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Alnwick Castle ( ) is a castle and country house in Alnwick in the English county of Northumberland. It is the seat of the 12th Duke of Northumberland, built following the Norman Conquest and renovated and remodelled several times.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most recognisable castles, featured in Harry Potter and Downton Abbey.

name: Bamburgh Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Bamburgh Castle, on the northeast coast of England, by the village of Bamburgh in Northumberland, is a Grade I listed building.
The site was originally the location of a Celtic Brittonic fort known as Din Guarie and may have been the capital of the kingdom of Bernicia from its foundation c.
why_interesting: A dramatic fortress perched high above the sweeping sands of the Northumberland coast.

name: Bywell Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bywell Castle is situated in the village of Bywell overlooking the River Tyne, four miles east of Corbridge, Northumberland, England (grid reference NZ049615). It is a Grade I listed building and a Scheduled Ancient Monument.
why_interesting: A remarkably intact Norman gatehouse overlooking the River Tyne.

name: Chillingham Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Chillingham Castle is a medieval castle in the village of Chillingham in the northern part of Northumberland, England. It was the seat of the Grey and Bennet (later Earls of Tankerville) families from the 15th century until the 1980s, when it became the home of Sir Edward Humphry Tyrrell Wakefield, 2nd Baronet, who is married to a member of the original Grey family.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most famous haunted castles, steeped in centuries of legend.

name: Dunstanburgh Castle
why_interesting: The spectacular cliff-top ruins of one of Northumberland's greatest medieval fortresses.

name: Etal Castle
why_interesting: A compact border fortress guarding the route into Scotland.

name: Langley Castle
why_interesting: England's only medieval castle hotel, beautifully restored within ancient walls.

name: Nottingham Castle
why_interesting: The impressive ducal fortress overlooking the city of Nottingham.

name: Broughton Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Broughton Castle is a medieval fortified manor house in the village of Broughton, which is about two miles (3 km) southwest of Banbury in Oxfordshire, England, on the B4035 road (grid reference SP418382).
It is the home of the Fiennes (in full Twisleton-Wykeham-Fiennes) family, Barons Saye and Sele.
why_interesting: A magnificent moated manor house that has remained in the same family for over 700 years.

name: Caus Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Caus Castle is a ruin of a hill fort and medieval castle in the civil parish of Westbury in the English county of Shropshire. It is situated up on the eastern foothills of the Long Mountain guarding the route from Shrewsbury, Shropshire to Montgomery, Powys, on the border between England and Wales.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a Norman border fortress in the Shropshire Hills.

name: Ludlow Castle
why_interesting: One of the finest medieval castles in England, overlooking the River Teme.

name: Shirburn Castle
why_interesting: A rare privately owned fortified mansion surrounded by parkland.

name: Shrewsbury Castle
why_interesting: The striking red sandstone castle overlooking the River Severn.

name: Wallingford Castle
why_interesting: The vast ruins of one of England's most powerful medieval castles.

name: Arundel Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Arundel Castle is a restored and remodelled medieval castle in Arundel, West Sussex, England. It was established by Roger de Montgomery in the 11th century.
why_interesting: One of England's most magnificent inhabited castles, overlooking the River Arun.

name: Bungay Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bungay Castle is a Grade I listed building in the town of Bungay, Suffolk.
why_interesting: The impressive Norman ruins overlooking the Waveney Valley.

name: Eccleshall Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Eccleshall Castle is located in Eccleshall, Staffordshire, England (grid reference SJ827295). It was originally built in the 13th century.
why_interesting: The ruined palace of the Bishops of Lichfield.

name: Framlingham Castle
why_interesting: The magnificent fortress where Mary Tudor was proclaimed Queen of England.

name: Hylton Castle
why_interesting: A beautifully restored gatehouse overlooking the River Wear.

name: Orford Castle
why_interesting: One of England's most distinctive polygonal keeps overlooking Orford Ness.

name: Tutbury Castle
why_interesting: The dramatic medieval fortress overlooking the River Dove.

name: Bolton Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bolton Castle is a 14th-century castle located in Wensleydale, Yorkshire, England (grid reference SE03379183). The nearby village of Castle Bolton takes its name from the castle.
why_interesting: One of England's finest preserved medieval castles, overlooking Wensleydale.

name: Broadway Tower, Worcestershire
Wikipedia Extract: Broadway Tower is an 18th-century building near the village of Broadway, in the English county of Worcestershire. It is a Grade II listed building.
why_interesting: A striking Gothic folly offering panoramic views across the Cotswolds.

name: Castle Hill, Mere
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Hill, also called Mere Castle, was a medieval fortification built by Richard, the Earl of Cornwall, in 1253 on a hill overlooking the town of Mere, Wiltshire, England. The castle was constructed in stone, with six towers, inner buildings and gates.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a Norman motte overlooking Mere.

name: Cawood Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Cawood Castle is a grade I listed building in Cawood, a village in North Yorkshire, England. The surviving fifteenth-century structures formed part of a fortified medieval palace belonging to the Archbishops of York, which was dismantled in the aftermath of the English Civil War.
why_interesting: The ruined palace of the Archbishops of York beside the River Ouse.

name: Skipsea Castle
why_interesting: The impressive earthworks of a Norman motte overlooking the Humber.

name: Wressle Castle
why_interesting: The magnificent ruins of one of Yorkshire's finest medieval castles.

name: Helmsley Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Helmsley Castle (also known anciently as Hamlake) is a medieval castle situated in the market town of Helmsley, within the North York Moors National Park, North Yorkshire, England.
why_interesting: The dramatic riverside ruins of a royal fortress overlooking Helmsley.

name: Knaresborough Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Knaresborough Castle is a ruined fortress overlooking the River Nidd in the town of Knaresborough, North Yorkshire, England.
why_interesting: A picturesque Norman castle overlooking the River Nidd.

name: Richmond Castle
why_interesting: One of Britain's greatest Norman castles, dominating the Yorkshire Dales.

name: Scarborough Castle
why_interesting: The spectacular headland fortress overlooking Scarborough's twin bays.

name: Upsall Castle
why_interesting: The historic seat of the Upsall family overlooking the Hambleton Hills.

name: Aboyne Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Aboyne Castle is a 13th-century castle in Aberdeenshire, Scotland  0.75 mi (1.21 km) north of the town of Aboyne (Grid Reference NO5299). The location of Aboyne Castle was selected for its strategic position near the River Dee and controlling the northern end of one of the Mounth crossings.
why_interesting: A magnificent Highland castle overlooking Royal Deeside and the River Dee.

name: Allardice Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Allardice Castle (also spelled Allardyce) is a sixteenth-century manor house in Kincardineshire, Scotland.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved Scottish tower house hidden in the Mearns countryside.

name: Balmoral Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Balmoral Castle ( bal-MORR-əl) is a large estate house in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, and a residence of the British royal family. It is near the village of Crathie, 9 miles (14 km) west of Ballater and 50 miles (80 km) west of Aberdeen.
why_interesting: The Scottish royal family's famous Highland residence set within the Cairngorms National Park.

name: Bognie Castle
why_interesting: The romantic ruins of a 12th-century castle overlooking the Aberdeenshire countryside.

name: Braemar Castle
why_interesting: A remarkably preserved 17th-century garrison castle at the heart of Braemar.

name: Castle Fraser
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Fraser is a large Z-plan castle near Kemnay, Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It is considered one of the most elaborate examples of its type and one of the grandest of the 'Castles of Mar'.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's grandest baronial castles, famed for its fairytale turrets and lavish interiors.

name: Corgarff Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Corgarff Castle is located slightly west of the village of Corgarff, in Aberdeenshire, north-east Scotland. It stands by the Lecht road, which crosses the pass between Strathdon and Tomintoul.
why_interesting: A striking star-shaped fortress standing high in the Cairngorms.

name: Craigievar Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Craigievar Castle is a harled castle or fortified country house 6 miles (9.7 km) south of Alford, Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It was the seat of Clan Sempill, and the Forbes family resided here for 350 years until 1963, when the property was sold to the National Trust for Scotland by the 19th Lord Sempill.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's most enchanting pink harled castles, straight from a storybook.

name: Crathes Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Crathes Castle (pronounced  KRATH-iss) is a castle built in the 16th century, near Banchory in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It is in the historic county of Kincardineshire.
why_interesting: A magnificent tower house surrounded by exquisite walled gardens and ancient yew hedges.

name: Delgatie Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Delgatie Castle is a castle near Turriff, in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. The castle consists of a white-harled, five-storey tower dating from the 16th century, with later extensions.
why_interesting: A welcoming medieval castle famed for its ghost stories and historic interiors.

name: Drum Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Drum Castle is a castle near Drumoak in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. For centuries it was the seat of the chief of Clan Irvine.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's oldest tower houses, surrounded by ancient oak woodland.

name: Dunnottar Castle
why_interesting: One of Britain's most spectacular castle ruins, dramatically perched above the North Sea.

name: Fyvie Castle
why_interesting: A magnificent Scottish castle renowned for its lavish interiors and ghostly legends.

name: Affleck Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Affleck Castle, also known as Auchenleck Castle, is a tall L-plan tower house dating from the 15th century, 4 miles (6.4 km) north of Monifieth and 1 mile (1.6 km) west of Monikie Parish Church, Angus, Scotland. It is a scheduled monument.
why_interesting: The picturesque ruins of a medieval tower house hidden in Angus.

name: Castle Newe
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Newe was a castellated mansion house, situated in Aberdeenshire, and designed in 1831 by Archibald Simpson. It was based on an existing Z-plan castle from 1604, which had square towers and was similar to Glenbuchat Castle.
why_interesting: A grand Victorian mansion standing on the site of an earlier castle.

name: Castle of Rattray
Wikipedia Extract: The Castle of Rattray was a medieval Scottish castle, with multiple variations on its structure over approximately six centuries. Originally built as a "late 12th- or early 13th century defensive motte" it provided protection for Starny Keppie Harbour and Rattray village.
why_interesting: The atmospheric ruins of a medieval castle swallowed by shifting sand dunes.

name: Inverallochy Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Inverallochy Castle is a ruined courtyard castle, near the village of Inverallochy in the Buchan area of North-East Scotland, dating to 1504. It lies 0.5 miles (0.80 km) south of Cairnbulg Castle, near Fraserburgh, and formerly stood beside the now-drained Loch of Inverallochy.
why_interesting: The striking ruins of a 16th-century tower house overlooking the Buchan coast.

name: Kindrochit Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Kindrochit Castle () is a ruined 14th-century fortification in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It is located at Braemar, in a strategic position on the banks of the Clunie Water, a tributary of the River Dee.
why_interesting: The ruined hunting lodge built by Malcolm III beside Braemar.

name: Kinnaird Head
Wikipedia Extract: Kinnaird Head (Scottish Gaelic: An Ceann Àrd, "high headland") is a headland projecting into the North Sea, within the town of Fraserburgh, Aberdeenshire, on the east coast of Scotland. The 16th-century Kinnaird Castle was converted in 1787 for use as the Kinnaird Head Lighthouse, the first lighthouse in Scotland to be lit by the Commissioners of Northern Lights.
why_interesting: A dramatic castle and lighthouse standing together on a rocky headland above the North Sea.

name: Muchalls Castle
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved Z-plan castle hidden in rural Aberdeenshire.

name: Tolquhon Castle
why_interesting: One of Scotland's finest Renaissance castles, famous for its elaborate stonework.

name: Balintore Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Balintore Castle is a Victorian Category A listed building in Scotland. The castle occupies an elevated site in moorland above Balintore village, a few miles north of the Loch of Lintrathen, near Kirriemuir, Angus.
why_interesting: A magnificent Gothic Revival mansion overlooking the Angus countryside.

name: Ballumbie
Wikipedia Extract: Ballumbie is a residential area on the north-east edge of Dundee, Scotland. The area was formerly an estate centred on Ballumbie Castle, a mid-16th-century fortification, which was followed by the 19th-century Ballumbie House.
why_interesting: An elegant Georgian mansion set within a historic Angus estate.

name: Brechin Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Brechin Castle is a castle in Brechin, Angus, Scotland. The castle was constructed in stone during the 13th century.
why_interesting: The historic seat of the Earls of Dalhousie overlooking the River South Esk.

name: Colliston Castle
why_interesting: The romantic ruins of a medieval tower house in the Angus countryside.

name: Finavon Castle
why_interesting: The picturesque remains of a royal hunting lodge in Glen Esk.

name: Alloa Tower
Wikipedia Extract: Alloa Tower in Alloa, Clackmannanshire, in central Scotland, is an early 14th-century tower house that served as the medieval residence of the Erskine family, later Earls of Mar. Retaining its original timber roof and battlements, the tower is one of the earliest and largest Scottish tower houses, with immensely thick walls.
why_interesting: Scotland's largest surviving medieval tower house, dominating the centre of Alloa.

name: Barholm Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Barholm Castle is a tower house located 5 miles (8.0 km) south-west of Gatehouse of Fleet, in Kirkcudbrightshire, Galloway, Scotland.
The tower dates back to the late 15th century, and it was a stronghold of a branch of the MacCulloch family.
why_interesting: A beautifully restored medieval tower house in the Galloway countryside.

name: Castle Stalker
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Stalker (Scottish Gaelic: Caisteal an Stalcaire) is a four-storey tower house or keep in the Scottish county of Argyll. It is set on a tidal islet on Loch Laich, an inlet off Loch Linnhe.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's most photographed castles, standing on its own tidal island.

name: Duntrune Castle
why_interesting: One of Scotland's oldest continuously inhabited castles overlooking Loch Crinan.

name: Gylen Castle
why_interesting: The dramatic ruins of a clifftop castle on the Isle of Kerrera.

name: Inveraray Castle
why_interesting: The spectacular ancestral home of the Dukes of Argyll overlooking Loch Fyne.

name: Kames Castle
why_interesting: The picturesque ruins of a medieval island castle on the Isle of Bute.

name: Kilmory Castle
why_interesting: A handsome Victorian mansion overlooking Loch Gilp.

name: Skipness Castle
why_interesting: A remarkably complete medieval fortress guarding the Kilbrannan Sound.

name: Torosay Castle
why_interesting: A grand Victorian baronial mansion overlooking the Isle of Mull.

name: Broughty Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Broughty Castle is a historic castle on the banks of the River Tay in Broughty Ferry, Dundee, Scotland. It was completed around 1495, although the site was earlier fortified in 1454, when George Douglas, 4th Earl of Angus, received permission to build on the site.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved artillery fortress overlooking the mouth of the River Tay.

name: Castle of St John
Wikipedia Extract: The Castle of St John, also known as Stranraer Castle, is an early 16th-century L-plan tower house in the centre of Stranraer, in Dumfries and Galloway, southwest Scotland. It was built by the Adairs of Kilhilt (who originally came from Ireland) c. 1510.
why_interesting: The imposing tower house overlooking the harbour at Stranraer.

name: Claypotts Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Claypotts Castle is a late medieval castle in the suburban West Ferry area of Dundee, Scotland.  It is one of the best-preserved examples of a 16th-century Z-plan tower house in Scotland.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's finest Z-plan castles, complete with its distinctive corner towers.

name: Closeburn Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Closeburn Castle is a privately owned tower house, probably of the 14th century, but possibly older, and is one of the oldest continually inhabited houses in Scotland. The castle is located 1 km east of the village of Closeburn, in the historical county of Dumfriesshire, 2 km south-east of Thornhill, in Dumfries and Galloway,  Scotland.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's oldest inhabited tower houses overlooking Nithsdale.

name: Comlongon Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Comlongon Castle is a tower house dating from the later 15th century or early 16th century. It is located 1 kilometre (0.6 mi) west of the village of Clarencefield, and 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) south-east of Dumfries, in south west Scotland.
why_interesting: A magnificent medieval castle now operating as a luxury hotel.

name: Drumlanrig Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Drumlanrig Castle is situated on the Queensberry Estate in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland. The category A listed castle is the Dumfriesshire home of the Duke of Buccleuch and Queensberry.
why_interesting: A spectacular ducal palace surrounded by one of Scotland's finest designed landscapes.

name: Sanquhar Castle
why_interesting: The romantic ruins of a medieval royal castle overlooking Sanquhar.

name: Bass Rock
Wikipedia Extract: The Bass Rock, or simply the Bass ( ), is an island in the outer part of the Firth of Forth in the east of Scotland. Approximately 2 km (1 mi) offshore, and 5 km (3 mi) north-east of North Berwick, it is a steep-sided volcanic plug, 107 m (351 ft) at its highest point, and is home to a large colony of gannets.
why_interesting: A dramatic volcanic island crowned by one of the world's largest gannet colonies.

name: Dean Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dean Castle is a 14th century castle located in Kilmarnock, East Ayrshire, Scotland. It was the stronghold for the Boyd Family, who were lords of Kilmarnock for over 400 years, and is situated in a 200-acre (80-hectare) site situated within the Dean Castle Country Park.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's finest urban castles, surrounded by beautiful parkland.

name: Dunbar Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dunbar Castle was one of the strongest fortresses in Scotland, situated in a prominent position overlooking the harbour of the town of Dunbar, in East Lothian.  Several fortifications were built successively on the site, near the English-Scottish border.
why_interesting: The ruined royal fortress overlooking the North Sea harbour at Dunbar.

name: Fa'side Castle
why_interesting: A beautifully restored medieval tower house overlooking East Lothian.

name: Loudoun Castle
why_interesting: The romantic Gothic Revival ruins of a once-grand Ayrshire castle.

name: Airth Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Airth Castle is a castle overlooking the village of Airth and the River Forth, in the Falkirk area of Scotland. Until 2023, the castle operated as a hotel and spa.
why_interesting: A magnificent baronial castle overlooking the River Forth.

name: Balgonie Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Balgonie Castle is located on the south bank of the River Leven near Milton of Balgonie, 3.5 kilometres (2.2 mi) east of Glenrothes, Fife, Scotland. The castle keep dates from the 14th century, and the remaining structures were added piecemeal until the 18th century.
why_interesting: A beautifully restored medieval tower house overlooking the River Leven.

name: Blackness Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Blackness Castle is a 15th-century fortress, near the village of Blackness, Scotland, on the south shore of the Firth of Forth.
It was built, probably on the site of an earlier fort, by Sir George Crichton in the 1440s.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's best-preserved artillery forts, dramatically jutting into the Firth of Forth.

name: Craigentinny
Wikipedia Extract:
Craigentinny is a suburb in the north-east of Edinburgh, Scotland, east of Restalrig and Lochend.
Its name may be a corruption of the Gaelic Creag an t-Sionnaich, meaning "the fox's rock".
why_interesting: A Gothic villa standing within Edinburgh's historic Craigentinny estate.

name: Craigmillar Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Craigmillar Castle is a ruined medieval castle in Edinburgh, Scotland. It is three miles (4.8 km) south-east of the city centre, on a low hill to the south of the modern suburb of Craigmillar.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's finest medieval castles, hidden within Edinburgh's suburbs.

name: Edinburgh Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Edinburgh Castle (Scottish Gaelic: Caisteal Dhùn Èideann) is a historic castle in Edinburgh, Scotland. It stands on Castle Rock, which has been occupied by humans since at least the Iron Age.
why_interesting: Scotland's iconic hilltop fortress dominating the Edinburgh skyline.

name: Merchiston Tower
why_interesting: The original fortified tower that gave Merchiston its name.

name: Ardvreck Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Ardvreck Castle is a castle, now ruinous, standing on a rocky promontory in Loch Assynt, Sutherland, Scotland, UK. The structure dates from about 1490 and is associated with the then landowners, the Macleods of Assynt.
why_interesting: The haunting ruins of a remote castle overlooking Loch Assynt.

name: Balnagown Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Balnagown Castle (also Balnagowan)(Ross Castle) is beside the village of Kildary in Easter Ross, part of the Highland area of Scotland.
There has been a castle on the site since the 14th century, although the present building was remodelled in the 18th and 19th centuries.
why_interesting: A magnificent Highland castle surrounded by ancient woodland.

name: Carbisdale Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Carbisdale Castle was built in 1907 for the Duchess of Sutherland on a hill across the Kyle of Sutherland from Invershin in the Scottish Highlands. From 1945 to 2011 it was used as a youth hostel, operated by the Scottish Youth Hostels Association.
why_interesting: A grand Baronial mansion overlooking the Kyle of Sutherland.

name: Crookston Castle
why_interesting: One of Glasgow's best-preserved medieval castles.

name: Falkland Palace
why_interesting: A magnificent royal palace that was once the favourite retreat of Scotland's monarchs.
