Wikipedia Extract: Faversham Stone Chapel also known as Our Lady of Elwarton, is a medieval chapel built on top of a Romano-British mausoleum. The chapel is located in what is thought to have been the Roman settlement of Durolevum, near the modern town of Faversham, in Kent, England.
why_interesting: The remains of a rare Romano-British roadside chapel.

name: Bannaventa
Wikipedia Extract: Bannaventa or Benaventa was a Romano-British fortified town which was on the Roman road later called Watling Street, which today is here, as in most places, the A5 road. Bannaventa straddles the boundaries of Norton and Whilton, Northamptonshire, England, villages highly clustered 1 kilometre (0.62 mi) and double that away, respectively.
why_interesting: The important Roman settlement on Watling Street.

name: Calleva Atrebatum
Wikipedia Extract: Calleva Atrebatum ("Calleva of the Atrebates") was an Iron Age oppidum, the capital of the Atrebates tribe. It then became a walled town in the Roman province of Britannia, at a major crossroads of the roads of southern Britain.
why_interesting: One of Britain's best-preserved Roman towns, enclosed by impressive defensive walls.

name: Camulodunum
Wikipedia Extract: Camulodunum ( KAM-(y)uu-loh-DEW-nəm; Latin: camvlodvnvm), the Ancient Roman name for what is now Colchester in Essex, was an important castrum and city in Roman Britain, and the first capital of the province. A temporary "strapline" in the 1960s identifying it as the "oldest recorded town in Britain" has become popular with residents and is still used on heritage roadsigns on trunk road approaches.
why_interesting: Britain's first Roman capital, with extensive archaeological remains beneath Colchester.

name: Letocetum
Wikipedia Extract: Letocetum is the ancient remains of a Roman settlement. It was an important military staging post and posting station near the junction of Watling Street, the Roman military road to north Wales, and Icknield (or Ryknild) Street (now the A38).
why_interesting: The important Roman settlement at Wall, complete with surviving bathhouse.

name: Lindinis
Wikipedia Extract: Lindinis or Lendiniae was a small walled town in the Roman province of Britannia Superior. The settlement developed around an early Roman fort.
why_interesting: The Roman town that once stood beneath modern Ilchester.

name: Mediolanum (Whitchurch)
Wikipedia Extract: Mediolanum was a fort and small town in the Roman province of Britannia. Today it is known as Whitchurch, located in the English county of Shropshire.
why_interesting: The Roman settlement beneath modern Whitchurch.

name: Noviomagus Reginorum
Wikipedia Extract: Noviomagus Reginorum was Chichester's Roman heart, very little of which survives above ground.  It lay in the land of the Atrebates and is in the early medieval-founded English county of West Sussex.
why_interesting: The Roman city beneath Chichester, once the capital of the Regni tribe.

name: Ratae Corieltauvorum
Wikipedia Extract: Ratae Corieltauvorum or simply Ratae was a town in the Roman province of Britannia. Today it is known as Leicester, located in the English county of Leicestershire.
why_interesting: The Roman city that became modern Leicester.

name: St Nicholas Church, Leicester
Wikipedia Extract: St Nicholas Church is an ancient Anglo-Saxon Church of England parish church in Leicester, England. One of the five surviving medieval churches of Leicester Old Town, it was constructed over 1150 years ago and is Leicester's oldest and longest continually used building.
why_interesting: One of Leicester's oldest churches, built within the Roman town walls.

name: Gelligaer
Wikipedia Extract: Gelligaer (Welsh: Gelli-gaer; Welsh pronunciation: [ˌɡɛɬɪˈɡaːɨr]) is a community in the County Borough of Caerphilly, Wales, in the Rhymney River valley. As well as the village of Gelligaer, the community also includes the small towns of Hengoed and Ystrad Mynach.
why_interesting: One of Britain's best-preserved Roman auxiliary forts in south Wales.

name: Jordan Hill Roman Temple
Wikipedia Extract: Jordan Hill Roman Temple is a Romano-Celtic temple and Roman ruin situated on Jordan Hill above Bowleaze Cove in the eastern suburbs of Weymouth in Dorset, England. Original amateur archaeological excavations on the site were carried out by J. Medhurst in 1843-6.
why_interesting: The remains of a rare Romano-Celtic temple overlooking Weymouth Bay.

name: Keston Roman villa
Wikipedia Extract: The Keston Roman villa is an archaeological site in Keston in the London Borough of Bromley, England.  The villa consisted of several buildings including a mausoleum.
why_interesting: The extensive remains of a Roman villa hidden within woodland.

name: Nunnery Mead
Wikipedia Extract: Nunnery Mead is a nature reserve of the Dorset Wildlife Trust, near Frampton and about 2 miles south-east of Maiden Newton, in Dorset, England. It is a former water-meadow, next to the River Frome.
why_interesting: The remains of a Romano-British villa beside the River Frome.

name: Rudston Roman villa
Wikipedia Extract: Rudston Roman villa is a Romano-British villa and scheduled monument near Rudston, East Riding of Yorkshire, England.
why_interesting: The mosaic-rich remains of a Roman villa in the Yorkshire Wolds.

name: Rutland Roman villa
Wikipedia Extract: The Rutland Roman villa is a Romano-British villa site near Ketton in Rutland, England. The site was listed as a scheduled monument by Historic England on 23 November 2021.
why_interesting: One of Britain's finest courtyard villas, with remarkable surviving mosaics.

name: Totternhoe Roman villa
Wikipedia Extract: Totternhoe Roman villa is on Church Farm, Church Road, in Totternhoe, Bedfordshire, England. No sign of it is now visible, as it has been filled in and grassed over.
why_interesting: The remains of an extensive Roman villa overlooking the Chiltern Hills.

name: Wanstead Roman Villa
Wikipedia Extract: Wanstead Roman Villa was a Roman villa on an unknown site in what is now Wanstead Park. Archaeological excavations carried out in 1985  indicated a Roman presence here from the 1st to the 5th century AD, but did not locate any specific site of a Roman villa.
why_interesting: The excavated remains of a substantial Roman villa in east London.

name: Bangor Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Bangor Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gadeiriol Bangor) is the cathedral church of Bangor, Gwynedd, Wales. It is dedicated to its founder, Saint Deiniol.
why_interesting: The oldest cathedral city in Wales, with origins dating back to the 6th century.

name: Brecon Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Brecon Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gadeiriol Aberhonddu), in the town of Brecon, Powys, is the cathedral of the Diocese of Swansea and Brecon in the Church in Wales and seat of the Bishop of Swansea and Brecon. Previously the church of Brecon Priory and then the Parish Church of St John the Evangelist, it became Brecon Cathedral following the disestablishment of the Church in Wales in 1920 and the creation of the diocese in 1923.
why_interesting: A magnificent Norman cathedral overlooking the River Usk.

name: Llandaff Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Llandaff Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gadeiriol Llandaf) is a Church in Wales cathedral and parish church in Llandaff, Cardiff, Wales. It is the seat of the Bishop of Llandaff, head of the Church in Wales Diocese of Llandaff.
why_interesting: One of Britain's finest medieval cathedrals, famed for its spectacular nave.

name: Newport Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Newport Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gaderiol Casnewydd/Cadeirlan Casnewydd), also known as St Gwynllyw's or St Woolos' Cathedral, is the cathedral of the Diocese of Monmouth within the Church in Wales, and the seat of the Bishop of Monmouth. Its official title is Newport Cathedral Church of St Woolos, King and Confessor.
why_interesting: The historic cathedral at the heart of Newport's medieval city.

name: St Asaph Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: The Cathedral Church of Saints Asaph and Cyndeyrn, commonly called St Asaph Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gadeiriol Llanelwy), is a Church in Wales cathedral in St Asaph, Denbighshire, north Wales. It is the episcopal seat of the Bishop of St Asaph.
why_interesting: Wales' smallest ancient cathedral, renowned for its medieval carvings.

name: St Davids Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: St Davids Cathedral (Welsh: Eglwys Gadeiriol Tyddewi) is a Church in Wales cathedral situated in St Davids, Britain's smallest city, in the county of Pembrokeshire, near the most westerly point of Wales.
why_interesting: The spiritual heart of Wales, built on the site of St David's monastery.

name: Church of St Mary the Virgin, Halkyn
Wikipedia Extract: The Church of St Mary the Virgin, Halkyn is to the north of the village of Halkyn, Flintshire, Wales.  It is an active Anglican parish church in the diocese of St Asaph.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved medieval church overlooking the Halkyn countryside.

name: Llanthony Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Llanthony Priory (Welsh: Priordy Llanddewi Nant Hodni) is a partly ruined former Augustinian priory in the secluded Vale of Ewyas, a steep-sided once-glaciated valley within the Black Mountains area of the Brecon Beacons National Park in Monmouthshire, south east Wales. It lies seven miles north of Abergavenny on an old road to Hay-on-Wye at Llanthony.
why_interesting: The spectacular ruins of a medieval priory hidden in the Black Mountains.

name: Priory Church of St Mary, Abergavenny
Wikipedia Extract:
The Priory Church of St Mary, Abergavenny is a parish church in the centre of Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, Wales.
St.
why_interesting: A magnificent Benedictine priory church in the heart of Abergavenny.

name: Priory Church of St Mary, Chepstow
Wikipedia Extract: The Parish and Priory Church of St Mary is located in Chepstow, Monmouthshire, south east Wales. Parts of the building, including its ornate west doorway, date from the late 11th century and are contemporary with the nearby Norman castle.
why_interesting: The impressive Norman priory beside Chepstow Castle.

name: St Baglan's Church, Llanfaglan
Wikipedia Extract: St Baglan's Church, Llanfaglan, is a redundant church in the parish of Llanfaglan, Gwynedd, Wales.  It is designated by Cadw as a Grade I listed building, and is under the care of the Friends of Friendless Churches.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved medieval church overlooking the Menai Strait.

name: St Brothen's Church, Llanfrothen
Wikipedia Extract: St Brothen's Church, Llanfrothen, is a redundant church at the edge of the village of Llanfrothen, Gwynedd, Wales.  It is designated by Cadw as a Grade I listed building because it is "a fine Medieval church retaining much of exterior and interior interest".
why_interesting: A picturesque medieval church beneath the mountains of Eryri.

name: Ewenny Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Ewenny Priory (Welsh: Priordy Ewenni), in Ewenny in the Vale of Glamorgan, Wales, was a monastery of the Benedictine order, founded in the 12th century. The priory was unusual in having extensive military-style defences and in its state of preservation; the architectural historian John Newman described it as “the most complete and impressive Norman ecclesiastical building in Glamorgan”.
why_interesting: One of Wales' best-preserved fortified priories, still serving as a parish church.

name: Maesyronnen Chapel
Wikipedia Extract: Maesyronnen Chapel is about 1 mile (2 km) north of the village of Glasbury, Powys, Wales (grid reference SO176410).  It is designated by Cadw as a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved 18th-century nonconformist chapel in the Brecon Beacons.

name: St Cadoc's Church, Cheriton
Wikipedia Extract:
The Church of St Cadoc, sometimes referred to as "The Cathedral of Gower", is a Grade I listed building and an Anglican church located in the hamlet of Cheriton on the north side of the Gower Peninsula, Wales, United Kingdom.
The present church was built in the 13th century and is believed to have replaced an earlier church within the manor of Landimore.
why_interesting: A remarkable medieval church on the Gower Peninsula with rare wall paintings.

name: All Saints' Church, Gresford
Wikipedia Extract: All Saints' Church (Welsh: Eglwys yr Holl Saint) stands in the former coal mining village of Gresford in Wrexham County Borough, Wales. It is a large, mainly late 15th-century church in a slightly red sandstone, in many ways more typical of nearby Cheshire churches.
why_interesting: One of northeast Wales' finest parish churches, famed for its soaring spire.

name: Church of St John the Baptist, Llanblethian
Wikipedia Extract: The Church of St John the Baptist is a medieval church in Llanblethian in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. Believed to have been built in the 12th century, the church boasts an unusual tower, consistent with the style more common in the south west of England.
why_interesting: A beautiful medieval church overlooking the River Thaw.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Marcross
Wikipedia Extract: Holy Trinity Church is a Grade I-listed church in Marcross (part of the community of St Donats), a village in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. It received its status as a Grade I-listed building on 22 February 1963.
why_interesting: A picturesque clifftop church overlooking the Glamorgan Heritage Coast.

name: St Augustine's Church, Penarth
Wikipedia Extract: St Augustine's Church (Welsh: Eglwys Sant Awstin) is a Grade I-listed Gothic Revival nineteenth-century parish church in Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, Wales.
why_interesting: Penarth's landmark Victorian parish church overlooking the Bristol Channel.

name: St Cadoc's Church, Llancarfan
Wikipedia Extract: St Cadoc's Church, Llancarfan is a church in Llancarfan, in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. It dates from the 13th century and has been a Grade I listed building since 28 January 1963.
why_interesting: One of Wales' most picturesque medieval churches, nestled beside the River Thaw.

name: St Chad's Church, Holt
Wikipedia Extract: St Chad's Church, Holt, is in the village of Holt, Wrexham County Borough, Wales overlooking the River Dee and the Wales–England border. It is an active Anglican church in the deanery of Alyn, the archdeaconry of Wrexham and the diocese of St Asaph.
why_interesting: A magnificent medieval church beside the River Dee.

name: St Donat's Church, St Donats
Wikipedia Extract: St Donat's Church (Welsh: Eglwys Sain Dunwyd) is a Grade I listed church in St Donats, in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. It became a Grade I listed building on 22 February 1963.
why_interesting: A striking medieval church overlooking St Donat's Castle.
Notes: Possible near-duplicate: "St Donat's Church, Welsh St Donats".

name: St Giles' Church, Wrexham
Wikipedia Extract:
St Giles' Parish Church (Welsh: Eglwys San Silyn) is the parish church of Wrexham, Wales. The church is recognised as one of the finest examples of ecclesiastical architecture in Wales and is a Grade I listed building, described by Sir Simon Jenkins as 'the glory of the Marches' and by W. D. Caröe as a “glorious masterpiece.”
The iconic 16th-century tower rises to a height of 41 m (136 feet) and is a local landmark that can be seen for many miles around.
why_interesting: One of Wales' finest medieval parish churches, home to the tallest medieval church tower in Wales.

name: St Illtyd's Church, Llantwit Major
Wikipedia Extract: St Illtyd's Church  is a church complex in Llantwit Major, Vale of Glamorgan, southeast Wales. It is located at the site of the oldest college in the United Kingdom, once believed to have been founded as Côr Tewdws c.
why_interesting: One of Britain's oldest Christian sites, with remarkable Celtic carved stones dating back over 1,000 years.

name: Amaravati Buddhist Monastery
Wikipedia Extract: Amaravati is a Theravada Buddhist monastery at the eastern end of the Chiltern Hills in South East England. Established in 1984 by Ajahn Sumedho as an extension of Chithurst Buddhist Monastery, the monastery has its roots in the Thai Forest Tradition.
why_interesting: Theravāda Buddhist monastery founded by Ajahn Sumedho, one of Europe's most important Buddhist centres.

name: Arthington Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Arthington Priory was an English monastery which was home to a community of nuns in Arthington, West Yorkshire, founded in the mid-12th century. The priory land is occupied by a residence called "Arthington Hall", which was built around 1585, and little, if anything, remains of the priory.
why_interesting: Ruins of a medieval Augustinian nunnery overlooking the River Wharfe.

name: Broadholme Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Broadholme Priory was a convent of canonesses of the Premonstratensian Order located near to the village of Broadholme. Historically in Nottinghamshire, since boundary changes in 1989, the priory and village has been in Lincolnshire.
why_interesting: Rare remains of a 12th-century Cistercian priory in rural Lincolnshire.

name: Carisbrooke Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Carisbrooke Priory was an alien priory, a dependency of Lyre Abbey in Normandy, France. The priory was situated on rising ground on the outskirts of Carisbrooke close to Newport on the Isle of Wight.
why_interesting: Historic Catholic priory founded in 1920 beside Carisbrooke Castle.

name: Chithurst Buddhist Monastery
Wikipedia Extract: Cittaviveka (Pali: 'discerning mind'), commonly known as Chithurst Buddhist Monastery, is an English Theravada Buddhist monastery in the Thai Forest Tradition. It is situated in West Sussex, England in the hamlet of Chithurst between Midhurst and Petersfield.
why_interesting: Peaceful Buddhist monastery set within the South Downs National Park.

name: Bath Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: The Abbey Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, commonly known as Bath Abbey, is a parish church of the Church of England and former Benedictine monastery in Bath, Somerset, England. Founded in the 7th century, it was reorganised in the 10th century and rebuilt in the 12th and 16th centuries; major restoration work was carried out by Sir George Gilbert Scott in the 1860s.
why_interesting: Magnificent Gothic church rebuilt in the 12th century, famous for its fan-vaulted ceiling and Abbey organ.

name: Buckfast Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Buckfast Abbey forms part of an active Benedictine monastery at Buckfast, near Buckfastleigh, Devon, England. Buckfast first became home to an abbey in 1018.
why_interesting: Working Benedictine monastery rebuilt from 1882, famous for Gregorian chant and monastic life.

name: Bisham Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Bisham Abbey is a Grade I listed manor house at Bisham in the English county of Berkshire. The name is taken from the now lost monastery which once stood alongside.
why_interesting: Former medieval abbey transformed into a Tudor mansion for Henry VIII's children.

name: Bristol Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Bristol Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, is a Church of England cathedral in the city of Bristol, England. It is the seat of the Bishop of Bristol.
why_interesting: One of England's great medieval churches, with a stunning Norman chapter house.

name: Bushmead Priory
Wikipedia Extract: The Priory Church of Saint Mary, Bushmead, commonly called Bushmead Priory, was a monastic foundation for Augustinian Canons, located at Bushmead (a hamlet in Staploe parish) in the County of Bedfordshire in England. It is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Well-preserved ruins of a small Augustinian priory founded around 1195.

name: Canons Ashby Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Canons Ashby Priory was an Augustinian priory at Canons Ashby, Northamptonshire, England.
why_interesting: Beautiful former Augustinian priory with a largely complete medieval church.

name: Carlisle Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Carlisle Cathedral, formally the Cathedral Church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity in Carlisle, is a Grade I listed Anglican cathedral in the city of Carlisle, Cumbria, England. It was founded as an Augustinian priory and became a cathedral in 1133.
why_interesting: Ancient cathedral founded in 1122, renowned for its spectacular medieval stained glass.

name: Cartmel Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Cartmel Priory is a former medieval Augustinian monastery in Cartmel, Cumbria, England (formerly in Lancashire). The priory's surviving church serves as the Anglican parish church of Cartmel.
why_interesting: Living medieval priory church at the heart of one of Cumbria's prettiest villages.

name: Kirkham Priory
Wikipedia Extract: The ruins of Kirkham Priory are situated on the banks of the River Derwent, at Kirkham, North Yorkshire, England. The Augustinian priory was founded in the 1120s by Walter l'Espec, lord of nearby Helmsley, who also built Rievaulx Abbey.
why_interesting: Atmospheric riverside ruins of a large Augustinian priory.

name: Lacock Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Lacock Abbey is a country house in the village of Lacock, Wiltshire, England. There was an abbey of nuns on the site until 1539, and the house is a remodelling and extension of the abbey's cloister court.
why_interesting: Medieval abbey transformed into a country house, later home to William Henry Fox Talbot, inventor of the photographic negative.

name: Lanercost Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Lanercost Priory was founded by Robert de Vaux between 1165 and 1174, the most likely date being 1169, to house Augustinian canons. The priory is situated in the village of Lanercost, Cumbria, England, within sight of Naworth Castle, with which it had close connections.
why_interesting: Impressive Augustinian priory beside Hadrian's Wall, with extensive medieval remains.

name: Launde Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Launde Abbey is located in Leicestershire, England, 14 miles east of the city of Leicester and 6 miles south west of Oakham in Rutland. The house was built on the site of the Augustinian Launde Priory.
why_interesting: Former Augustinian priory now operating as a Christian retreat.

name: Alcester Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Alcester Abbey was a Benedictine monastery in Alcester, Warwickshire in England, founded in 1138 by the Botellers of Oversley, Warwickshire. Its many endowments included the Chapel of St.
why_interesting: Ruins of a Benedictine abbey founded by Ralph le Boteler in the 12th century.

name: Alvecote Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Alvecote Priory is a ruined Benedictine priory in Alvecote, Warwickshire, England. The site has been scheduled as an ancient monument.
why_interesting: Ruined Augustinian priory founded around 1159 beside the River Anker.

name: Battle Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Battle Abbey is a partially ruined Benedictine abbey in Battle, East Sussex, England. The abbey was built on the site of the Battle of Hastings and dedicated to St Martin of Tours.
why_interesting: Built on the battlefield where William the Conqueror defeated King Harold in 1066.

name: Beadlow Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Beadlow Priory was a monastic foundation established between 1140 and 1146 by Robert D'Albini for a community of Benedictine monks.
why_interesting: Quiet Augustinian priory with surviving medieval earthworks and chapel remains.

name: Birkenhead Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Birkenhead Priory is in Priory Street, Birkenhead, Merseyside, England. It is the oldest standing building on Merseyside.
why_interesting: England's oldest standing monastic buildings, founded in 1150 overlooking the Mersey.

name: Boxgrove Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Boxgrove Priory is a ruined priory in the village of Boxgrove in Sussex, England. It was founded in the 12th century.
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved small Benedictine priories, with impressive Norman architecture.

name: Canterbury Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Canterbury Cathedral is the cathedral of the archbishop of Canterbury, the spiritual leader of the Church of England and symbolic leader of the worldwide Anglican Communion. Located in Canterbury, Kent, it is on the site of one of the oldest Christian structures in England and forms part of a World Heritage Site.
why_interesting: Seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury and one of Christianity's most important pilgrimage sites.

name: Castle Acre Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Acre Priory was a Cluniac priory in the village of Castle Acre, Norfolk, England, dedicated to St Mary, St Peter, and St Paul. It is thought to have been founded in 1089 by William de Warenne, 2nd Earl of Surrey (the son of the 1st Earl of Surrey who had founded England's first Cluniac priory at Lewes in 1077).
why_interesting: One of England's finest Norman monastic ruins, founded in 1090.

name: Denny Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Denny Abbey is a former abbey near Waterbeach, about 6 miles (10 km) north of Cambridge in Cambridgeshire, England. It is now the Farmland Museum and Denny Abbey.
why_interesting: Remarkably preserved Benedictine abbey and former farmhouse with links to the Denny family.

name: Downside Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Downside Abbey was a Benedictine monastery in England and is the senior community of the English Benedictine Congregation. Until 2019, the community had close links with Downside School, for the education of children aged 11 to 18.
why_interesting: Working Benedictine monastery renowned for its magnificent Gothic church.

name: Lindisfarne
Wikipedia Extract: Lindisfarne, also known as Holy Island, is a tidal island off the northeast coast of England, which constitutes the civil parish of Holy Island in Northumberland. Holy Island has a recorded history from the 6th century AD; it was an important centre of Celtic Christianity under Saints Aidan, Cuthbert, Eadfrith, and Eadberht of Lindisfarne.
why_interesting: Historic monastery on Holy Island, birthplace of the Lindisfarne Gospels and early English Christianity.

name: Bradwell Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Bradwell Abbey or Bradwell Priory is a scheduled monument and urban studies site in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire, England. It was a Benedictine priory, founded around 1154 and dissolved in 1524.
why_interesting: Former Benedictine abbey at the heart of Milton Keynes' medieval origins.

name: Reading Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Reading Abbey is a large, ruined abbey in the centre of the town of Reading, in the English county of Berkshire. It was founded by Henry I in 1121 "for the salvation of my soul, and the souls of King William, my father, and of King William, my brother, and Queen Maud, my wife, and all my ancestors and successors." In its heyday the abbey was one of Europe's largest royal monasteries.
why_interesting: Magnificent royal abbey founded by Henry I in 1121, now extensive atmospheric ruins.

name: Axholme Charterhouse
Wikipedia Extract: Axholme Charterhouse or Axholme Priory, also Melwood Priory or Low Melwood Priory, North Lincolnshire, is one of the ten medieval Carthusian houses (charterhouses) in England. It was established in 1397/1398 by Thomas Mowbray, Earl of Nottingham and later Duke of Norfolk.
why_interesting: England's only surviving Carthusian monastery site.

name: Beauvale Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Beauvale Priory (also known as Beauvale Charterhouse) was a Carthusian monastery in Beauvale, Nottinghamshire.
why_interesting: Ruins of a 14th-century priory founded by Nicholas de Cantelupe.

name: Byland Abbey
Wikipedia Extract:
Byland Abbey is a ruined abbey and a small village in Byland with Wass civil parish, in the county of North Yorkshire, England, in the North York Moors National Park.
From 1974 to 2023 it was part of Ryedale District, it is now administered by the unitary North Yorkshire Council.
why_interesting: Among England's finest Cistercian ruins, dramatically set beneath the Hambleton Hills.

name: Croxden Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Croxden Abbey, also known as "Abbey of the Vale of St. Mary at Croxden", was a Cistercian abbey at Croxden, Staffordshire, United Kingdom.
why_interesting: Substantial Cistercian abbey founded in 1176, surrounded by Staffordshire countryside.

name: Bromholm Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Bromholm Priory was a Cluniac priory, situated in a coastal location near the village of Bacton, Norfolk, England. It is Grade I listed.
why_interesting: Ruins of one of Norfolk's richest medieval priories, famous for its pilgrimage shrine.

name: Delapré Abbey
Wikipedia Extract:
Delapré Abbey is a neo-classical mansion in Northampton, England.
The mansion and outbuildings incorporate remains of a former monastery, the Abbey of St Mary de la Pré (the suffix meaning "in or of the Meadow"), near the River Nene, 1 mile (1.6 km) south southeast  of the centre of Northampton.
why_interesting: Former Cluniac priory transformed into one of Northamptonshire's finest country houses.

name: Monk Bretton Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Monk Bretton Priory is a ruined medieval priory located in the village of Lundwood, and close to Monk Bretton, South Yorkshire, England.
why_interesting: Well-preserved ruins of a Cluniac monastery overlooking the Dearne Valley.

name: Abbotskerswell Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Abbotskerswell Priory, on the outskirts of the village of Abbotskerswell, near Newton Abbot, Devon, England, was the home of a community of Augustinian nuns from 1861 until 1983. It has now been converted into apartments for retirees.
why_interesting: Historic priory founded in 1861, still home to an active Augustinian community.

name: Barrow Camera
Wikipedia Extract:
Barrow Camera was a Knights Hospitaller foundation in the parish of Barrow upon Trent, Derbyshire, England.
A Camera is: "A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Hospitallers for administrative purposes on their estates."
Barrow Camera was in the hamlet of Arleston in the parish of Barrow upon Trent in Derbyshire, however, several historians have mistaken it for the village of Barrow in Cheshire.
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved medieval camera buildings, once the administrative centre of Garendon Abbey.

name: Blackfriars, Gloucester
Wikipedia Extract:
Blackfriars, Gloucester, England, founded about 1239, is one of the most complete surviving Dominican black friaries in England.
Now owned by English Heritage and restored in 1960, it is currently leased to Gloucester City Council and used for weddings, concerts, exhibitions, guided tours, filming, educational events and private hires.
why_interesting: Outstanding Dominican friary with one of Britain's finest surviving medieval cloisters.

name: Blackfriars, Newcastle upon Tyne
Wikipedia Extract: Blackfriars is a restored Grade I listed 13th-century former priory in Newcastle upon Tyne, Tyne and Wear, England, located in the city centre, close to the city's Chinatown.
why_interesting: Medieval Dominican friary preserving one of England's best surviving friary churches.

name: Blackfriars, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: Blackfriars Priory (formally the Priory of the Holy Spirit) is a Dominican religious community in Oxford, England. Its primary work is the administration of two educational institutions: Blackfriars Studium, a centre of theological studies in the Roman Catholic tradition; and Blackfriars Hall, a constituent permanent private hall of the University of Oxford.
why_interesting: Home of Oxford's Dominican community since 1221, beside the historic city centre.

name: Bayham Old Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Bayham Old Abbey is an English Heritage property, located near Lamberhurst, Kent, England. Founded c.
why_interesting: Picturesque ruins of a Premonstratensian abbey in the Kent countryside.

name: Beeleigh Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Beeleigh Abbey near Maldon in Essex, England, was a monastery constructed in 1180 for the Premonstratensians, as known as the Norbertines or Premonstratensians. The order linked the change of the separate life of monks in the 12th century with the retrospective life of the friar, who was considerably more active.
why_interesting: Former Premonstratensian abbey converted into an elegant country house.

name: Bridgwater Friary
Wikipedia Extract:
Bridgwater Friary was a Franciscan monastery in Bridgwater, Somerset, England, established in 1245 and dissolved in 1538.
It was founded by William Briwere and moved from another location.
why_interesting: Rare surviving Franciscan friary remains in Somerset.

name: Castle Hedingham Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Hedingham Priory was a Benedictine nunnery in Castle Hedingham, Essex, founded in or before 1190 by Aubrey de Vere, 1st Earl of Oxford, perhaps in partnership with his third wife, Agnes of Essex.  It was dedicated to the Virgin Mary, St.
why_interesting: Small medieval priory closely linked to Hedingham Castle.

name: Egglestone Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Egglestone Abbey is a ruined Premonstratensian abbey in County Durham, England. It is 1+1⁄2 miles (2.4 km) southeast of Barnard Castle, on the south bank of the River Tees, and was historically within the North Riding of Yorkshire.
why_interesting: Beautiful riverside ruins of a Premonstratensian abbey beside the River Tees.

name: Forde Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Forde Abbey is a privately owned former Cistercian monastery in Dorset, England. The house and gardens are run as a tourist attraction while the 1,600-acre (650 ha) estate is farmed to provide additional revenue.
why_interesting: Magnificent former Cistercian abbey transformed into a grand country house.

name: Gorton Monastery
Wikipedia Extract: The Church and Friary of St Francis, known locally as Gorton Monastery, is a Grade II* listed former Franciscan friary on Gorton Lane in Gorton, an area of Manchester, England. It was designed by the Victorian architect Edward Welby Pugin and built between 1866 and 1872.
why_interesting: Spectacular Gothic monastery completed in 1904, one of Manchester's architectural masterpieces.

name: Baddesley Preceptory
Wikipedia Extract: Baddesley Preceptory was a preceptory of the Knights Hospitaller at North Baddesley in Hampshire, England. The preceptory was founded at Godsfield but was moved soon after the Black Death.
why_interesting: Knights Hospitaller preceptory founded around 1199, among Hampshire's oldest monastic sites.

name: Farmcote Grange
Wikipedia Extract:
Farmcote Grange was a medieval monastic grange at Farmcote in Gloucestershire, England.
It was a grange of Hailes Abbey.
why_interesting: Former medieval grange of Hailes Abbey in the Cotswolds.

name: Franciscan Friary, Southampton
Wikipedia Extract: The Franciscan Friary of Southampton was founded c. 1233.
why_interesting: Important medieval Franciscan friary with surviving archaeological remains.

name: Appuldurcombe House
Wikipedia Extract: Appuldurcombe House (also spelt Appledorecombe or Appledore Combe) is the shell of a large 18th-century English Baroque country house of the Worsley family. The house is situated near to Wroxall on the Isle of Wight, England.
why_interesting: Grand 18th-century house built on the site of a dissolved medieval priory.

name: Aslackby Preceptory
Wikipedia Extract: Aslackby Preceptory in Lincolnshire lay to the south-east of Aslackby Church. Until about 1891 a tower, possibly of the preceptory church, together with a vaulted undercroft, survived as part the Temple farmhouse.
why_interesting: Rare remains of a Knights Templar preceptory founded before 1164.

name: Barlings Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Barlings Abbey was one of nine Premonstratensian monasteries in the county of Lincolnshire, England.  It was founded in 1154, as a daughter house of the Abbey of St.
why_interesting: Extensive ruins of a wealthy Cistercian abbey founded in 1154.

name: Cockersand Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Cockersand Abbey is a former abbey and former civil parish near Cockerham in the City of Lancaster district of Lancashire, England. It is situated near the mouth of the River Cocker.
why_interesting: Remote Cistercian abbey dramatically overlooking Morecambe Bay.

name: Croxton Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Croxton Abbey, near Croxton Kerrial, Leicestershire, was a Premonstratensian monastery founded by William I, Count of Boulogne.
why_interesting: Ruins of a small Augustinian priory founded in the 12th century.

name: Boston Priory
Wikipedia Extract:
Boston Priory was a priory  in Boston, Lincolnshire, England.
The origins of St Botolph's Church, Boston have their roots in the former priory church of the Benedictine monastery.
why_interesting: One of England's oldest parish churches, originally founded as a medieval priory.

name: Bottesford Preceptory
Wikipedia Extract: Bottesford Preceptory was sited at Bottesford, just to the south of Scunthorpe, in Lindsey, England. It was on low-lying land, near the Bottesford Beck, about 3 miles (5 km) to the west of the escarpment of the Lincoln Cliff limestone upland, and about the same distance to the east of the River Trent.
why_interesting: Rare Knights Hospitaller preceptory founded in the 12th century, with surviving medieval earthworks.

name: Bridgend Priory
Wikipedia Extract:
Bridgend Priory was a monastic house in Horbling, Lincolnshire, England.
The priory was founded around 1199 by Godwin the Rich of Lincoln, a benefactor to the Gilbertine Order of Sempringham Priory.
why_interesting: Small medieval priory in rural Lincolnshire with a quiet riverside setting.

name: Burwell Priory
Wikipedia Extract:
Burwell Priory was a priory in the village of Burwell, Lincolnshire, England.
The priory was built around 1110 for Benedictine monks, by Ansgot of Burwell, who addressed his charter to Robert, Bishop of Lincoln 1094-1123.
why_interesting: Former Benedictine priory with surviving medieval remains beside St Mary's Church.

name: Cammeringham Priory
Wikipedia Extract:
Cammeringham Priory was a priory in Cammeringham, Lincolnshire, England, and was one of nine Premonstratensian houses in the historical county.
It was an Alien house granted by 1126 to the abbey of L'Essay in the diocese of Coutances, by Robert de Haya, with the advice of his wife Muriel, and also to the Premonstratensian abbey of Blanchelande in Normandy.
why_interesting: Little-known medieval priory founded around 1148 in rural Lincolnshire.

name: Haverholme Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Haverholme Priory was a former monastery and a country house in Lincolnshire, England. Its remains are situated 4 miles (6 km) north-east of the town of Sleaford and less than 1 mile (1.6 km) south-west from the village of Anwick.
why_interesting: Ruins of a once-powerful Gilbertine priory dissolved by Henry VIII in 1539.

name: Lesnes Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Lesnes Abbey  is a former abbey, now ruined, in Abbey Wood, in the London Borough of Bexley, south-east London, England. It is a scheduled monument, and the abbey's ruins are listed at Grade II by Historic England.
why_interesting: Atmospheric ruins of a 12th-century Augustinian abbey overlooking the Thames marshes.

name: Balsall Preceptory
Wikipedia Extract: Balsall Preceptory in Warwickshire was a manor that was given to the Knights Templars in recognition of their service in the Crusades. The donor, according to a survey of the Templars' possessions in England in 1185, was Roger de Mowbray, son of Nigel d'Aubigny.
why_interesting: Knights Templar preceptory founded before 1250, with substantial earthwork remains.

name: Beauchief Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Beauchief Abbey is a medieval monastic house now serving as a parish church in the southern suburbs of Sheffield, England.
why_interesting: Former Premonstratensian abbey founded in 1176, now one of Sheffield's oldest surviving buildings.

name: Chichester Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Chichester Cathedral, formally known as the Cathedral Church of the Holy Trinity, is the seat of the Anglican Bishop of Chichester. It is located in Chichester, in West Sussex, England.
why_interesting: Seat of the Diocese of Chichester, renowned for its detached medieval bell tower and Marc Chagall stained-glass window.

name: Erdington Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Erdington Abbey Church (grid reference SP112922) on Sutton Road, Erdington, Birmingham, England, is the more usual name of the grade II listed church of Saints Thomas and Edmund of Canterbury. It is the church of a Roman Catholic parish in the Archdiocese of Birmingham served by the Redemptorists.
why_interesting: Benedictine monastery founded in 1876, still home to an active monastic community.

name: Bar Convent
Wikipedia Extract: The Bar Convent Living Heritage Centre, at Micklegate Bar, York, England, established in 1686, is the oldest surviving Catholic convent in the British Isles. The laws of England at this time prohibited the foundation of Catholic convents and as a result of this, the convent was both established and operated in secret.
why_interesting: England's oldest surviving convent, founded in 1686 and still occupied by religious sisters.

name: Basingwerk Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Basingwerk Abbey (Welsh: Abaty Dinas Basing) is a Grade I listed ruined abbey near Holywell, Flintshire, Wales. The abbey, which was founded in the 12th century, belonged to the Order of Cistercians.
why_interesting: Important Cistercian abbey founded in 1131 beside the River Dee.

name: Bolton Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Bolton Abbey Estate in Wharfedale, North Yorkshire, England, takes its name from a 12th-century Augustinian monastery of canons regular, technically a priory, which was closed in the 1539 Dissolution of the Monasteries ordered by King Henry VIII. It is in the Yorkshire Dales, next to the village of Bolton Abbey. The estate belongs to the Duke of Devonshire.
why_interesting: Ruined Augustinian priory in spectacular Wharfedale, now one of Yorkshire's best-loved beauty spots.

name: Margam Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Margam Abbey (Welsh: Abaty Margam) was a Cistercian monastery, located in the village of Margam, a suburb of modern Port Talbot in Wales. The nave of the abbey church is still in use as the church of St Mary in the Church in Wales.
why_interesting: Former Cistercian abbey transformed into the magnificent church within Margam Country Park.

name: Neath Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Neath Abbey (Welsh: Abaty Nedd) was a Cistercian monastery, located near the present-day town of Neath in South Wales, UK. It was once the largest abbey in Wales. Substantial ruins can still be seen, and are in the care of Cadw.
why_interesting: Extensive ruins of one of Wales' richest medieval Cistercian monasteries.

name: Selby Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Selby Abbey is a former Benedictine abbey and current Anglican parish church in the town of Selby, North Yorkshire, England. It is a member of the Major Churches Network in England.
why_interesting: Magnificent Benedictine abbey founded in 1069, crowned by one of England's finest Norman towers.

name: Strata Florida Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Strata Florida Abbey (Welsh: Abaty Ystrad Fflur; ) is a former Cistercian abbey situated just outside Pontrhydfendigaid, near Tregaron in the county of Ceredigion, Wales. The abbey was founded in 1164.
why_interesting: Remote Welsh abbey founded in 1164, once the spiritual centre of medieval Wales.

name: Barnwell Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Barnwell Castle is a ruined castle, south of the town of Oundle, and north of the village of Barnwell, Northamptonshire (grid reference TL047853).  It has been designated by English Heritage as a Grade I listed building, and is a Scheduled Ancient Monument.
why_interesting: Well-preserved fortified manor house with corner towers and a medieval moat.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bourn Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Bourn Castle was in the village of Bourn in Cambridgeshire, 10 miles to the west of Cambridge (grid reference TL322562).
It originally consisted of wooden buildings on an earthwork enclosure which was erected by Picot of Cambridge around 1080, which was towards the end of the reign of William the Conqueror.
why_interesting: Substantial Norman motte-and-bailey castle built soon after the Norman Conquest.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Dalton Castle, Cumbria
Wikipedia Extract: Dalton Castle is a Grade I listed 14th-century peel tower in Dalton-in-Furness, Cumbria, England. Constructed during a period of Scottish raids on Furness, it served as the administrative and judicial centre of the lordship of Furness Abbey, functioning as a courthouse and prison as well as a defensive structure.
why_interesting: Unique 14th-century tower keep built to defend the Furness peninsula.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cooling Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Cooling Castle is a 14th-century quadrangular castle in the village of Cooling, Kent on the Hoo Peninsula about 6 miles (9.7 km) north of Rochester. It was built in the 1380s by the Cobham family, the local lords of the manor, to guard the area against French raids into the Thames Estuary.
why_interesting: Perfectly preserved 14th-century gatehouse built to protect the Thames Estuary.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Dunster Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dunster Castle is a former motte and bailey castle, now a country house, in the village of Dunster, Somerset, England. The castle lies on the top of a steep hill called the Tor, and has been fortified since the late Anglo-Saxon period.
why_interesting: National Trust castle continuously occupied for over 1,000 years, blending Norman, medieval and Victorian architecture.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Amberley Castle
Wikipedia Extract:
Amberley Castle stands in the village of Amberley, West Sussex (grid reference TQ027132).
The castle was erected as a 12th-century manor house and fortified in 1377, giving it a rhomboid shaped stonework enclosure with high curtain walls, internal towers in each corner, a hall and a gateway.
why_interesting: Luxury hotel occupying a beautifully restored medieval castle dating from 1103.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bitchfield Tower
Wikipedia Extract: Bitchfield Tower or West Bitchfield Tower is a medieval pele tower near Belsay, Northumberland, England. It is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Rare surviving medieval tower house on the Anglo-Scottish border.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bramber Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bramber Castle is the ruins of a Norman motte-and-bailey castle, formerly the caput of the large feudal barony of Bramber long held by the Braose family. It is situated in the village of Bramber, West Sussex, near the town of Steyning, overlooking the River Adur.
why_interesting: Norman castle ruins commanding sweeping views across the Adur Valley.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Alford Manor House
Wikipedia Extract: The Manor House is a Grade II* listed building which can be found on West street within Alford, Lincolnshire, England. It is believed to be the largest thatched manor house in England and was built to a traditional H plan in 1611.
why_interesting: Lincolnshire's largest thatched manor house, dating from 1611.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Beaudesert, Cannock Chase
Wikipedia Extract: Beaudesert was an estate and stately home on the southern edge of Cannock Chase in Staffordshire. It was one of the family seats of the Paget family, the Marquesses of Anglesey.
why_interesting: Former great country estate on Cannock Chase, now surviving mainly through its landscaped site and ruins.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Beaupré Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Beaupré Hall was a large 16th-century house mainly of brick, which was built by the Beaupres in Outwell, Norfolk, England and enlarged by their successors the Bells. Like many of Britain's country houses it was demolished in the mid-20th century.
why_interesting: Historic Norfolk country house with Tudor origins and distinctive brick architecture.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Belhus, Essex
Wikipedia Extract: Belhus is a golf course, country park, former stately home and manor in the parish of Aveley in Essex, England. The historic manor was known in medieval times variously as "Bellhouse, Belhouse (as commemorated by today's "Belhouse Avenue" in the village of Aveley), Bell House", etc.
why_interesting: Former Essex country estate whose parkland survives as Belhus Woods Country Park.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Clumber Park
Wikipedia Extract: Clumber Park is a country park in The Dukeries near Worksop in the civil parish of Clumber and Hardwick, Nottinghamshire, England. The estate, which was the seat of the Pelham-Clintons, Dukes of Newcastle, was purchased by the National Trust in 1946.
why_interesting: Vast historic estate of parkland, woodland and lake, once centred on a grand ducal mansion.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Astley Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Astley Castle  is a ruinous moated fortified 16th century manor house in North Warwickshire, England. It has been a Grade II* listed building since 1952 and a Scheduled Ancient Monument since 1994.
why_interesting: Medieval moated castle ruins imaginatively restored as a modern residence.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Avebury Manor and Garden
Wikipedia Extract: Avebury Manor & Garden is a National Trust property consisting of a Grade I listed early-16th-century manor house and its surrounding garden. It is in Avebury, near Marlborough, Wiltshire, England, in the centre of the village next to St James's Church and close to the Avebury neolithic henge monument.
why_interesting: Historic manor and gardens beside Avebury's world-famous prehistoric stone circle.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Baguley Hall
Wikipedia Extract:
Baguley Hall is a 14th-century timber-framed building in Baguley, Greater Manchester, England.
A former country house, historically in Cheshire, it is now Grade I listed and a Scheduled Ancient Monument.
why_interesting: One of Manchester's oldest surviving timber-framed manor houses.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bank Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Bank Hall is a Jacobean mansion in Bretherton, Lancashire, England. It is a Grade II* listed building and is at the centre of its own private estate, surrounded by parkland.
why_interesting: Atmospheric Jacobean mansion whose ruins preserve the scale of a once-grand Lancashire estate.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Birmingham Manor House
Wikipedia Extract: The Birmingham Manor House or Birmingham Moat was a moated building that formed the seat of the Lord of the manor of Birmingham, England during the Middle Ages, remaining the property of the de Birmingham family until 1536. The buildings were demolished and the moat filled-in in 1815–16, but the remains of medieval stone structures excavated in 1973–75 survive intact beneath the buildings of the Birmingham Wholesale Markets.
why_interesting: Site of Birmingham's lost medieval manor house, once the centre of the de Birmingham family's estate.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cothelstone Manor
Wikipedia Extract:
Cothelstone Manor in Cothelstone, Somerset, England was built in the mid-16th century, largely demolished by the parliamentary troops in 1646 and rebuilt by E.J. Esdaile in 1855–56.
It is closely associated with the Church of St Thomas of Canterbury, which is a Grade I listed building, and contains memorials to many of the owners of Cothelstone Manor including: Sir Matthew de Stawell, died 1379, and his wife Elizabeth, and John Stawell, died 1603.
why_interesting: Historic Somerset manor with medieval origins and a remarkable Tudor great hall.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cranham Hall
Wikipedia Extract:
Cranham Hall is a Grade II listed building in Cranham, London, England.
Built c.1795, it forms a typical Essex church-manor house complex, standing on the ridge in the south of the former parish of Cranham.
why_interesting: Historic Essex country-house site reflecting Cranham's rural estate past.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: East Barsham Manor
Wikipedia Extract: East Barsham Manor is an important work of Tudor architecture, a leading and early example of a prodigy house, originally built in the 1520s. It is located in the village of East Barsham, about 2.5 miles (4.1 km) north of the town of Fakenham and 2.1 miles (3.4 km) south west of the village of Walsingham in the English county of Norfolk.
why_interesting: Outstanding Tudor brick manor built around 1520, renowned for its ornate chimneys.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Eastbury Manor House
Wikipedia Extract: Eastbury Manor House is a Grade I listed building situated in the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham in Greater London, England. It dates to the Elizabethan period, although the land on which it was built was formerly part of the demesne of Barking Abbey.
why_interesting: Rare Elizabethan merchant's house in London, surrounded by restored period gardens.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Fitz Manor
Wikipedia Extract: Fitz Manor is a manor house in the village of Fitz near Montford Bridge, Shropshire, England. It is a Grade II* listed building.
why_interesting: Historic Shropshire timber-framed manor associated with the Fitz family.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: High Sunderland Hall
Wikipedia Extract: High Sunderland Hall was a medieval manor house clad in stone c. 1600.
why_interesting: Ruined Elizabethan mansion commanding views across the Calder Valley.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Hinxworth Place
Wikipedia Extract:
Hinxworth Place is a medieval manor house near Hinxworth, Hertfordshire, England.
Formerly the Manor of Pulters, building was started c.
why_interesting: Grade I listed late-medieval manor house in rural Hertfordshire.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Iford Manor
Wikipedia Extract: Iford Manor (grid reference ST802589) is a manor house in Wiltshire, England. It is a Grade II* listed building sitting on the steep, south-facing slope of the Frome valley, in Westwood parish, about 2 miles (3.2 km) southwest of the town of Bradford-on-Avon.
why_interesting: Italianate manor garden designed by Harold Peto, celebrated for terraces, sculpture and valley views.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Kemerton Court
Wikipedia Extract:
Kemerton Court is the principal manor house of the village of Kemerton, near Tewkesbury in Gloucestershire.
The house is built of local Cotswold stone, dating from the late 16th century onwards.
why_interesting: Historic Worcestershire country house in a village beneath Bredon Hill.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Langdon Court, Devon
Wikipedia Extract: Langdon Court is a former manor house, in Wembury, South Devon, England. It consists of a  single courtyard mansion from 1693 and a walled formal garden.
why_interesting: Historic South Devon manor house set in countryside near Plymouth Sound.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Edith Weston
Wikipedia Extract: Edith Weston is a village and civil parish in the county of Rutland in the East Midlands of England. The population of the civil parish was 1,042 at the 2001 census, including Normanton and increasing to 1,359 at the 2011 census.
why_interesting: A Rutland village beside Rutland Water rather than a stately home; this row may need recategorising.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Eggington House
Wikipedia Extract: Eggington House is the manor house of the village of Eggington situated near Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, England. The house is regarded as a very fine example of late 17th-century domestic architecture, and is a Grade II* listed building.
why_interesting: Historic Georgian country house set within a small Bedfordshire village.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Hinwick House
Wikipedia Extract: Hinwick House is a Grade I-listed Queen Anne country house located about 90 minutes from Central London, near Podington in North Bedfordshire. The estate consists of the Queen Anne main house, the Victorian wing, the Victorian wing extension, garage block, stables, three cottages attached to a clock tower, a walled garden and a period dovecote.
why_interesting: Grand Georgian mansion set in extensive Bedfordshire parkland.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Houghton House
Wikipedia Extract: Houghton House is a ruined mansion house in the parish of Houghton Conquest, Bedfordshire. It is a Grade I listed building, positioned above the surrounding countryside, and commands excellent views.
why_interesting: Roofless Jacobean hunting lodge with panoramic countryside views.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Aldermaston Court
Wikipedia Extract: Aldermaston Court is a country house and private park built in the Victorian era for Daniel Higford Davall Burr with incorporations from a Stuart house. It is south-east of the village nucleus of Aldermaston in the English county of Berkshire.
why_interesting: Historic Berkshire country house overlooking the Kennet Valley.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Billingbear House
Wikipedia Extract: Billingbear House was an English country house situated in the parish of Waltham St. Lawrence in Berkshire, England, about six miles from Windsor.
why_interesting: Historic Berkshire country-house site surrounded by former estate parkland.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Ascott House
Wikipedia Extract: Ascott House, sometimes referred to as simply Ascott, is a Grade II* listed building in the hamlet of Ascott near Wing in Buckinghamshire, England. It is set in a 32-acre / 13 hectare estate.
why_interesting: Arts and Crafts country house filled with collections assembled by the Rothschild family.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Aston Clinton House
Wikipedia Extract: Aston Clinton House (also known as Green Park though referred to as simply Aston Clinton by the Rothschild family) was a large mansion to the south-east of the village of Aston Clinton in Buckinghamshire, England.
why_interesting: Former Rothschild country house whose landscaped parkland survives in Buckinghamshire.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Foxhill House
Wikipedia Extract: Foxhill House is a Gothic Revival style building on what is now the Whiteknights campus of the University of Reading at Earley, adjoining the English town of Reading. It currently houses the university's School of Law.
why_interesting: Flamboyant Victorian Gothic mansion in Reading's Whiteknights Park.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Frogmore House
Wikipedia Extract: Frogmore House is a 17th-century English country house owned by the Crown Estate. It is a historic Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Historic royal retreat within Windsor Home Park, associated with generations of the Royal Family.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Prospect Park, Reading
Wikipedia Extract: Prospect Park is a public park in the western suburbs of Reading situated north of the Bath Road in the English county of Berkshire. It is the largest park in Reading, and includes a large regency style house, now known as Prospect Park Mansion House and previously as Prospect House.
why_interesting: Reading's historic public park, laid out around an 18th-century country house.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Royal Lodge
Wikipedia Extract: Royal Lodge is a Grade II listed house in Windsor Great Park in Berkshire, England, half a mile north of Cumberland Lodge and 3.2 miles (5.1 km) south of Windsor Castle. The site of homes since the 17th century, the present structure dates from the 19th century, and was expanded in the 1930s for the then Duke of York, the future King George VI. Its central section consists of three storeys, with two-storey wings, totalling about 30 rooms, including seven bedrooms.
why_interesting: Private royal residence within Windsor Great Park, long associated with the Royal Family.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Boarstall
Wikipedia Extract: Boarstall is a village and civil parish in the Buckinghamshire district of Buckinghamshire, England. It is in the Aylesbury Vale area about 12 miles (19 km) west of Aylesbury.
why_interesting: Fortified medieval manor site with a remarkable surviving gatehouse and earthworks.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Chequers
Wikipedia Extract: Chequers or Chequers Court ( CHEK-ərz) is the country house of the prime minister of the United Kingdom. A 16th-century manor house, it lies near the village of Ellesborough, halfway between the towns of Princes Risborough and Wendover in Buckinghamshire, at the foot of the Chiltern Hills, 40 miles (64 km) north-west of Central London.
why_interesting: The Prime Minister's official country residence since 1921, set in the Chiltern Hills.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Claydon House
Wikipedia Extract: Claydon House is a country house in mid-Buckinghamshire, England, near the village of Middle Claydon. It was built between 1757 and 1771 and is now owned by the National Trust.
why_interesting: 18th-century country house famed for lavish Rococo interiors and Verney family history.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cliveden
Wikipedia Extract: Cliveden (pronounced ) is an English country house and estate in the care of the National Trust in Buckinghamshire, on the border with Berkshire. The Italianate mansion, also known as Cliveden House, crowns an outlying ridge of the Chiltern Hills close to the South Bucks villages of Taplow and Burnham.
why_interesting: Clifftop mansion overlooking the Thames, famed for Astor society, political intrigue and the Profumo affair.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Eythrope
Wikipedia Extract: Eythrope (previously Ethorp) is a hamlet and country house in the parish of Waddesdon, in Buckinghamshire, England. It is located to the south east of the main village of Waddesdon.
why_interesting: Rothschild estate celebrated for Alice de Rothschild's remarkable walled garden, glasshouses and productive orchards.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Anglesey Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Anglesey Abbey is a National Trust property in the village of Lode, 5+1⁄2 miles (8.9 km) northeast of Cambridge, England. The property includes a country house, built on the remains of a priory, 98 acres (400,000 m2) of gardens and landscaped grounds, and a working mill.
why_interesting: Former 12th-century priory transformed into Lord Fairhaven's elegant home, with gardens and a working watermill.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Burghley House
Wikipedia Extract: Burghley House () is a grand 16th-century English country house near Stamford, Lincolnshire. It is a leading example of the Elizabethan prodigy house, built and still lived in by the senior (Exeter) branch of the Cecil family and is Grade I listed.
why_interesting: Elizabethan prodigy house built for William Cecil, Elizabeth I's chief adviser, and crowned by 76 chimneys.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cherry Hinton Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Cherry Hinton Hall is a house and park in Cherry Hinton, to the south of Cambridge, England. The house and grounds are owned and managed by Cambridge City Council.
why_interesting: Victorian country house whose park has hosted the Cambridge Folk Festival since 1965.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Adlington Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Adlington Hall is a country house near Adlington, Cheshire. The oldest part of the existing building, the Great Hall, was constructed between 1480 and 1505; the east wing was added in 1581.
why_interesting: Historic manor whose Great Hall contains a rare organ built around 1670 by Bernard Smith.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Arley Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Arley Hall is a country house in the village of Arley, Cheshire, England, about 4 miles (6 km) south of Lymm and 5 miles (8 km) north of Northwich.  It is home to the owner, Viscount Ashbrook, and his family.
why_interesting: Celebrated gardens featuring one of England's earliest double herbaceous borders, recorded on an 1846 plan.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Crewe Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Crewe Hall is a Jacobean mansion located near Crewe Green, east of Crewe, in Cheshire, England. Described by Nikolaus Pevsner as one of the two finest Jacobean houses in Cheshire, it is listed at grade I. Built in 1615–36 for Sir Randolph Crewe, it was one of the county's largest houses in the 17th century, and was said to have "brought London into Cheshire".
why_interesting: Jacobean mansion completed in 1636, dramatically restored after a devastating fire in 1866.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Doddington Hall, Cheshire
Wikipedia Extract: Doddington Hall is a country house in Doddington Park in the civil parish of Doddington, Cheshire, England.  It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Samuel Wyatt-designed mansion combining Georgian elegance, Capability Brown parkland and a surviving medieval tower.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Dorfold Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Dorfold Hall (SJ635524) is a Grade I listed Jacobean mansion in Acton, Cheshire, England, considered by Nikolaus Pevsner to be one of the two finest Jacobean houses in the county. The present owners are the Roundells.
why_interesting: Built from 1616 for an anticipated visit by James I, which apparently never happened.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Eaton Hall, Cheshire
Wikipedia Extract: Eaton Hall is the country house of the Duke of Westminster.  It is 1 mile (2 km) south of the village of Eccleston in Cheshire, England.
why_interesting: Ancestral seat of the Dukes of Westminster, set within one of Cheshire's grandest private estates.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Lower Carden Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Lower Carden Hall is a historic house in the civil parish of Carden, Cheshire, England.  It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Grade I-listed manor incorporating a 15th-century timber-framed farmhouse with medieval royal connections.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Lyme Park
Wikipedia Extract: Lyme Park is a large estate south of Disley, Cheshire, England. It is managed by the National Trust and consists of a mansion house surrounded by formal gardens and a deer park in the Peak District National Park.
why_interesting: Grand deer-park mansion instantly recognisable as Pemberley from the BBC's 1995 Pride and Prejudice.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Manor House, Hale
Wikipedia Extract: The Manor House, Hale is a house in Church End, Hale,  a village in the borough of Halton, Cheshire, England.  It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade II* listed building.
why_interesting: Grade II*-listed manor preserving the character of Hale's historic Cheshire village.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bonython Manor

Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Shotwick House
Wikipedia Extract: Shotwick House (originally known as Shotwick Park) is a large house in Great Saughall, Cheshire, England.  It is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade II listed building.
why_interesting: Victorian country estate distinguished by a John Douglas-designed stable courtyard.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cotehele
Wikipedia Extract: Cotehele is a medieval house with Tudor additions, situated in the parish of Calstock in the east of Cornwall, England, and now belonging to the National Trust. It is a rambling granite and slate-stone manor house on the banks of the River Tamar that has been little changed over five centuries.
why_interesting: Atmospheric Tudor house with medieval roots, rare tapestries and unusual whale-jawbone displays.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Godolphin Estate
Wikipedia Extract: The Godolphin Estate is a National Trust property situated in Godolphin Cross, 7 km (4.3 mi) north-west of Helston in Cornwall, England. The house is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: Ancient Cornish estate shaped by tin-mining wealth and 5,000 years of human activity.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Mount Edgcumbe House
Wikipedia Extract:
Mount Edgcumbe House is a stately home in south-east Cornwall and is a Grade II listed building, whilst its gardens and parkland are listed as Grade I in the Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England.
Mount Edgcumbe Country Park is situated in the parish of Maker on the Rame Peninsula, overlooking Plymouth Sound; its main entrance is in the village of Cremyll.
why_interesting: Tudor house built around 1547 specifically to command sweeping views across Plymouth Sound.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Pencarrow
Wikipedia Extract: Pencarrow is a Grade II*-listed country house in the civil parish of Egloshayle, in north Cornwall, England. It is situated three miles (5 km) east-southeast of Wadebridge and three miles (5 km) north-northwest of Bodmin.
why_interesting: Georgian mansion remaining with the same family for roughly 500 years.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Penhallam
Wikipedia Extract: Penhallam is the site of a fortified manor house near Jacobstow in Cornwall, England. There was probably an earlier, 11th-century ringwork castle on the site, constructed by Tryold or his son, Richard fitz Turold in the years after the Norman invasion of 1066.
why_interesting: Rare ground-plan remains of a 13th-century moated manor abandoned during the Middle Ages.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Abbey House, Barrow-in-Furness
Wikipedia Extract:
Abbey House on Abbey Road, Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria, England is a Neo-Elizabethan H-plan mansion designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and completed in 1914 as a guest house for Vickers Ltd and a flat for the Managing Director, Sir James McKechnie.
It takes its name from the adjacent Furness Abbey.
why_interesting: Arts and Crafts house designed by Edwin Lutyens for a director of the Vickers shipyard.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Brantwood
Wikipedia Extract: Brantwood is a historic house museum in Cumbria, England, overlooking Coniston Water. It has been the home to a number of prominent individuals.
why_interesting: John Ruskin's former home, filled with his art and overlooking Coniston Water.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Brougham Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Brougham Hall is a historic house museum located in the village of Brougham just outside Penrith, Cumbria, England.
why_interesting: Country-house ruins linked to secret wartime Canal Defence Light trials visited by Churchill and Eisenhower.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Clifton Hall, Cumbria
Wikipedia Extract: Clifton Hall was a fortified manor house in the village of Clifton, Cumbria. Dating from around 1400, it was constructed by either Elianor Engaine or her son-in-law William Wybergh, and was held by the Wybergh family until the 19th century.
why_interesting: Medieval pele tower plundered before the 1745 Battle of Clifton Moor, England's last land battle.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Barlborough Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Barlborough Hall is a Grade I listed 16th-century country house in Barlborough, Chesterfield, Derbyshire. It was built in around 1583-84 for Sir Francis Rodes and is attributed to Robert Smythson.
why_interesting: Elizabethan country house built for the influential Rodes family, with historic gardens and a garden pavilion.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Breadsall Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Breadsall Priory is a former Augustinian priory in Derbyshire, situated around two kilometres north of Breadsall, and two kilometres east of Little Eaton. The priory was established before 1266 by a member of the Curzon family.
why_interesting: Country-house hotel on a medieval priory site where scientist Erasmus Darwin died in 1802.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bretby Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Bretby Hall is a country house at Bretby, Derbyshire, England, north of Swadlincote and east of Burton upon Trent on the border with Staffordshire. It is a Grade II listed building.
why_interesting: Castellated Gothic mansion designed by Jeffry Wyatville for the Earls of Chesterfield.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Chatsworth House
Wikipedia Extract: Chatsworth House is a stately home in the Derbyshire Dales, 4 miles (6.4 km) north-east of Bakewell and 9 miles (14 km) west of Chesterfield, England. The seat of the Duke of Devonshire, it has belonged to the Cavendish family since 1549.
why_interesting: Cavendish family seat renowned for its art collection and starring as Pemberley in the 2005 film.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Holker Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Holker Hall (pronounced Hooker by some) is a privately owned country house located about 2 km to the south-west of the village of Cartmel in the ceremonial county of Cumbria and historic county of Lancashire, England. It is "the grandest [building] of its date in Lancashire ...by the best architects then living in the county." The building dates from the 16th century, with alterations, additions, and rebuilding in the 18th and 19th centuries.
why_interesting: Historic Cavendish family home rebuilt after an 1871 fire, with celebrated gardens and an ancient lime tree.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Derwent House, Matlock
Wikipedia Extract: Derwent House is a historic building in Matlock in Derbyshire, England, originally the home of the important Knowles family in the 17th century. The original estate included several buildings surrounding what is now known as Derwent House, including one which is believed to be one of the oldest buildings in Matlock, dating from circa 1670, predated only by the bridge over the River Derwent.
why_interesting: 1753 country house associated with local lead-mining wealth and grounds landscaped by Joseph Paxton.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Ednaston Manor
Wikipedia Extract: Ednaston Manor is a country house in Ednaston, near Brailsford, Derbyshire, England. It was built in 1912–19 in a Queen Anne style by Edwin Lutyens, for William G. Player.
why_interesting: Lutyens-designed Arts and Crafts manor, built from 1912 and praised as one of his finest houses.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Foremarke Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Foremarke Hall is a Georgian-Palladian country house and manor house. Completed in 1762, the Hall is located at the manor (hamlet) of Foremark, near the hamlets of Ingleby, Ticknall, Milton, and the village of Repton in South Derbyshire, England.
why_interesting: Elegant Palladian mansion built in 1755, later becoming the home of Repton Preparatory School.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Haddon Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Haddon Hall is an English country house on the River Wye near Bakewell, Derbyshire, a former seat of the Dukes of Rutland. It is the home of Lord Edward Manners (brother of the incumbent Duke) and his family.
why_interesting: Remarkably preserved medieval and Tudor hall, held by one family for more than 900 years.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Hardwick Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Hardwick Hall is an architecturally significant Elizabethan-era country house in Derbyshire, England. A leading example of the Elizabethan prodigy house, the Renaissance style home was built between 1590 and 1597 for Bess of Hardwick to a design of the architect Robert Smythson.
why_interesting: Bess of Hardwick's spectacular Elizabethan statement house, famously described as “more glass than wall”.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Kedleston Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Kedleston Hall is a large English country house with a Palladian exterior and Neo-classical interiors, now owned by the National Trust, built in the 1760s as the seat of the Curzon family, near Kedleston in Derbyshire, England, approximately 4 miles (6 km) north-west of Derby. The medieval village of Kedleston was moved in 1759 by Nathaniel Curzon to make way for the manor.
why_interesting: Robert Adam's neoclassical masterpiece, conceived as a grand temple to architecture and the arts.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: A la Ronde
Wikipedia Extract: A la Ronde is an 18th-century, 16-sided cottage orné near Lympstone, Exmouth, Devon, England, in the ownership of the National Trust. The house was built for two spinster cousins, Jane and Mary Parminter.
why_interesting: Extraordinary 16-sided house built in 1796, famous for its delicate shell-encrusted gallery.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Arlington Court
Wikipedia Extract: Arlington Court is a neoclassical style country house built 1820–23, situated in the parish of Arlington, next to the parish church of St James, 5+1⁄4 miles NE of Barnstaple, north Devon, England. It is a Grade II* listed building.
why_interesting: Regency family estate housing the National Trust's carriage collection and a rare William Blake drawing.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Buckland-Tout-Saints
Wikipedia Extract: Buckland-Tout-Saints is a village and civil parish in the South Hams district of Devon, England.  In the 2001 census it had a population of 178, up from a population of only 37 in 1901.
why_interesting: Georgian country house in wooded South Devon parkland, built on a much older manor site.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cadhay
Wikipedia Extract: Cadhay is an historic estate in the parish of Ottery St Mary in Devon, England, 10 miles (16 km) east of Exeter and 5 miles (8 km) from the sea at Sidmouth. The mansion house known as Cadhay House, 1 mile (2 km) north-west of Ottery St Mary village, is a grade I listed Elizabethan building.
why_interesting: Tudor manor built in 1550 around the Court of the Sovereigns, displaying four monarch statues.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Dartington Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Dartington Hall in Dartington, near Totnes, Devon, England, is an historic house and country estate of around 800 acres (320 hectares) dating from medieval times. The group of late 14th century  buildings are Grade I listed;  described in Pevsner's Buildings of England as "one of the most spectacular surviving domestic buildings of late Medieval England", along with Haddon Hall and Wingfield Manor.
why_interesting: Medieval hall transformed from 1925 into a pioneering international centre for arts, education and social reform.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Kingston Lacy
