Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Blythswood House
Wikipedia Extract:
Blythswood House was a 100-room neoclassical mansion at Renfrew, Scotland, built for the Douglas-Campbell family from the considerable incomes arising from their ownership of the Lands of Blythswood in Glasgow, including Blythswood Hill, developed initially by William Harley of Blythswood Square, and earlier lands surrounding Renfrew and Inchinnan.
It was designed in 1821, by the architect James Gillespie Graham for Archibald Campbell, the Member of Parliament for the Glasgow District of Burghs.
why_interesting: Former Renfrewshire mansion and seat of the Campbells of Blythswood, demolished in the 20th century.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Lambroughton
Wikipedia Extract: Lambroughton is a village in the old Barony of Kilmaurs, Scotland. This is a rural area famous for its milk and cheese production and the Ayrshire or Dunlop breed of cattle.
why_interesting: Historic Ayrshire estate recorded from the medieval period, now surviving mainly through its landscape and place-name.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Lands of Ashgrove
Wikipedia Extract: The Lands of Ashgrove, previously known as Ashenyards, formed a small estate in the Parish of Kilwinning, North Ayrshire, lying between Kilwinning and Stevenston. The Georgian mansion house was demolished in 1960, the substantial walled garden survives.
why_interesting: Long-established Ayrshire estate whose history survives mainly through local records and the surrounding landscape.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Lands of Cocklebie
Wikipedia Extract: The Lands of Cocklebie or Cocklebee formed an estate possessing a common border with the estates of Lainshaw, the Corsehill, and the town of Stewarton, East Ayrshire, Parish of Stewarton, Scotland.
why_interesting: Historic Ayrshire lands associated with the region's medieval and early modern farming estates.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Orangefield House, South Ayrshire
Wikipedia Extract: Orangefield House, previously known as 'Monkton House', was located near the village of Monkton, Ayrshire in the Parish of Monkton and Prestwick in South Ayrshire, Scotland; the settlement borders upon Glasgow Prestwick Airport, for which it served for a while as the control tower.
why_interesting: Historic Ayrshire country house representing the region's 18th-century estate culture.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Panmure House
Wikipedia Extract: Panmure House was a 17th-century country house in the Parish of Panbride, Angus, Scotland, 4 miles (6 km) to the north of Carnoustie. It was the seat of the Earl of Panmure.
why_interesting: Lost seat of the Earls of Panmure, demolished in the 20th century after centuries of family ownership.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Thorntoun house and estate
Wikipedia Extract: Thorntoun School was opened by Barnardo's in September 1971 for children with emotional difficulties aged 11 to 16 years. The school closed in 1990 and Thorntoun is now a nursing home.
why_interesting: Historic Ayrshire estate whose principal house was later adapted for educational use.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Tullichewan
Wikipedia Extract: Tullichewan is a former estate in the Vale of Leven, near Loch Lomond, Scotland. Tullichewan Castle was built in 1792 and demolished in 1954.
why_interesting: Demolished country mansion whose former estate survives near Balloch and Loch Lomond.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bodelwyddan Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Bodelwyddan Castle (Welsh: Castell Bodelwyddan), close to the village of Bodelwyddan, near Rhyl, Denbighshire in Wales, was built around 1460 by the Humphreys family of Anglesey as a manor house. It was associated with the Williams-Wynn family for around 200 years from 1690.
why_interesting: Victorian Gothic castle containing collections connected with Welsh portraiture and military history.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bodnant Garden
Wikipedia Extract:
Bodnant Garden (Welsh: Gardd Bodnant) is a National Trust property near Tal-y-Cafn, Conwy, Wales, overlooking the Conwy valley towards the Carneddau mountains.
Founded in 1874 and developed by five generations of one family, it was given to the National Trust in 1949.
why_interesting: World-famous garden celebrated for its Laburnum Arch, botanical collections and sweeping Conwy Valley views.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bodysgallen Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Bodysgallen Hall is a manor house in Conwy county borough, north Wales, near the village of Llanrhos. Since 2008 the house has been owned by the National Trust.
why_interesting: Historic country house incorporating a medieval tower and overlooking Conwy Castle and Snowdonia.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Bronwydd Castle

name: Gwrych Castle

why_interesting: Romantic Gothic Revival castle rescued from dereliction and used for television productions including I'm a Celebrity.

name: Gwydir Castle

name: Hawarden Castle (18th century)
Wikipedia Extract: (New) Hawarden Castle (Welsh: Castell Penarlâg (Newydd)) is a house in Hawarden, Flintshire, Wales. It was the estate of the former British prime minister William Ewart Gladstone, having previously belonged to the family of his wife, Catherine Glynne.

name: Hensol Castle

why_interesting: Seventeenth-century mansion overlooking a lake, now used as a hotel and events venue.

name: Kinmel Hall

why_interesting: Monumental 19th-century mansion known as the Welsh Versailles for its lavish French-inspired design.

name: Oxwich Castle

why_interesting: Tudor courtyard manor designed to resemble a castle, overlooking the Gower coast.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Penally Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Penally Abbey is an old rectory, now the Penally Abbey Country House Hotel and Restaurant overlooking Carmarthen Bay in the village of Penally, about 1.5 miles from Tenby, Pembrokeshire, Wales. It was once owned by the Jameson family of Irish whiskey distillers.
why_interesting: Gothic country house and hotel occupying a site associated with an early religious settlement.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Penrhyn Castle

why_interesting: Vast neo-Norman mansion built from Penrhyn slate wealth, with opulent interiors and difficult colonial connections.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cefnllys Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Cefnllys Castle (Welsh: Castell Cefn-llys, pronounced [ˈkastɛɬ kɛvn ɬɨːs]) was a medieval spur castle in Radnorshire (now part of Powys), Wales. Two successive masonry castles were built on a ridge above the River Ithon known as Castle Bank (Welsh: Craig y Castell, lit. 'castle rock') in the thirteenth century, replacing a wooden motte-and-bailey castle constructed by the Normans nearby.
why_interesting: Two medieval castle sites crown this dramatic hill above a loop of the River Ithon.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Aberglasney

why_interesting: Restored historic gardens famed for their cloister garden, pools and rediscovered Renaissance layout.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Baron Hill, Anglesey
Wikipedia Extract: Baron Hill is a country estate in Beaumaris, Anglesey, Wales. The ruined Baron Hill House and the associated Baron Hill Park were established in 1618 by Sir Richard Bulkeley as the family seat of the influential Bulkeley family.
why_interesting: Ruined Georgian mansion that served as the Anglesey seat of the Bulkeley family.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Llanerchaeron
Wikipedia Extract: Llanerchaeron,  known as "Llanayron House" to its nineteenth-century occupants, is a grade I listed mansion on the River Aeron, designed and built in 1795 by John Nash for Major (later Colonel) William Lewis as a model self-sufficient farm complex located near Ciliau Aeron, some 2+1⁄2 miles south-east of Aberaeron, Ceredigion, Wales. why_interesting: Elegant John Nash-designed villa preserving its service courtyard, walled gardens and working farm.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Cefntilla Court
Wikipedia Extract: Cefntilla Court, (also Cefn Tilla), Llandenny, Monmouthshire, Wales, is a country house dating from the mid-19th century. Its origins date from 1616.
why_interesting: Country house acquired for Lord Raglan's family after his death during the Crimean War.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Clytha Park
Wikipedia Extract: Clytha Park, Clytha, Monmouthshire, is a 19th-century Neoclassical country house, "the finest early nineteenth century Greek Revival house in the county." The wider estate encompasses Monmouthshire's "two outstanding examples of late eighteenth century Gothic", the gates to the park and Clytha Castle. The owners were the Jones family, later Herbert, of Treowen and Llanarth Court.
why_interesting: Neoclassical country house standing within an estate known for the nearby Clytha Castle folly.
Good For: history lovers, couples, family, day trip

name: Dewstow House
Wikipedia Extract: Dewstow House, Caldicot, Monmouthshire, Wales, is an early nineteenth century villa in a Neoclassical style. The building itself is plain; described by architectural writer John Newman as a "simple three-bay villa", it has extensive views over the Severn Estuary.
why_interesting: Extraordinary Victorian gardens rediscovered after decades underground, revealing grottoes, tunnels and ornamental pools.

name: Dundrennan Abbey

why_interesting: The Romanesque ruins where Mary, Queen of Scots spent her last night on Scottish soil.

name: Dunfermline Abbey

name: Craigie Castle

why_interesting: A little-visited ruined fortification with an unusually large vaulted hall.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Crossraguel Abbey

why_interesting: Extensive, well-preserved Cluniac abbey ruins near Maybole, one of Scotland's finest monastic sites.

name: Dryburgh Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Dryburgh Abbey, near Dryburgh on the banks of the River Tweed in the Scottish Borders, was nominally founded on 10 November (Martinmas) 1150 in an agreement between Hugh de Morville, Constable of Scotland, and the Premonstratensian canons regular from Alnwick Abbey in Northumberland. why_interesting: Set among ancient cedar trees, these red-stone ruins are the burial place of Sir Walter Scott.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Jedburgh Abbey

why_interesting: One of the finest ruined abbeys in the Scottish Borders, founded by King David I.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Kelso Abbey

It was founded in the 12th century by a community of Tironensian monks first brought to Scotland in the reign of Alexander I. It occupies ground overlooking the confluence of the Tweed and Teviot waters, the site of what was once the Royal Burgh of Roxburgh and the intended southern centre for the developing Scottish kingdom at that time.
why_interesting: Once the largest and richest of the Border abbeys, now reduced to a single dramatic tower.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Melrose Abbey

It was founded in 1136 by Cistercian monks at the request of King David I of Scotland and was the chief house of that order in the country until the Reformation.
why_interesting: Beautifully carved pink sandstone ruins said to hold the buried heart of Robert the Bruce.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Midhope Castle

why_interesting: A 16th-century tower house better known to many as 'Lallybroch' from the Outlander TV series.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Aberystwyth Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Aberystwyth Castle (Welsh: Castell Aberystwyth) is a Grade I listed Edwardian fortress located in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, Mid Wales. It was built in response to the First Welsh War in the late 13th century, replacing an earlier fortress located a mile to the south.
why_interesting: A ruined Edwardian fortress on a headland, with sweeping views over Cardigan Bay.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Cilgerran Castle

why_interesting: A dramatic ruined castle perched above a gorge on the River Teifi, said to have inspired Turner's paintings.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Abbey of Kells
Wikipedia Extract: The Abbey of Kells (Irish: Mainistir Cheanannais) or Kells Priory is a former monastery in Kells, County Meath, Ireland, 59 kilometres (37 mi) north-west of Dublin. why_interesting: The ruined priory and round tower in the town famed for the medieval illuminated Book of Kells.
Good For: history lovers, walkers and hikers, photographers

name: Abbeydorney Abbey

The abbey was the daughter-house of Monasteranenagh in County Limerick, and was the only medieval Cistercian house in County Kerry.
why_interesting: Atmospheric abbey ruins with a strong sense of history and place.

name: Athassel Priory

name: Ballybeg Priory

why_interesting: Atmospheric abbey ruins with a strong sense of history and place.

why_interesting: A ruined 15th-century friary in Killarney National Park, its cloister centred on an ancient yew tree.

name: Red Abbey, Cork

name: Avebury

why_interesting: A smaller stone circle within easy reach of Callanish, rarely visited compared to its famous neighbour.

name: Callanish Stones

The Calanais Stones (also known as Calanais I; Scottish Gaelic: Clachan Chalanais or Tursachan Chalanais) are a prehistoric stone circle and stone alignment on the west coast of the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland. The monument was built during the Neolithic period, around c. 2750 BC.
The stones form a circle with a tall central monolith and several rows of standing stones extending outward in different directions, creating a distinctive cross-shaped layout.

why_interesting: A remote Bronze Age stone ring on Shetland, its name meaning 'limping dance' after a folk tale of trolls turned to stone.

name: Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings
Wikipedia Extract: Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings is an open-air museum of rescued buildings which have been relocated to its site in Stoke Heath, a district of Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, England.  Founded in 1963 and opened in 1967, the museum was conceived following the dismantling of a 15th-century timber-framed house in Bromsgrove in 1962 to provide a location for its reconstruction.
why_interesting: A fascinating museum where historic windmills and rural buildings have been rescued and rebuilt.

name: Chesterton Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: Chesterton Windmill is a 17th-century cylindric stone tower windmill with an arched base, located outside the village of Chesterton, Warwickshire. It is a Grade I listed building and a striking landmark in south-east Warwickshire.
why_interesting: One of England's most photographed windmills, standing alone on a Warwickshire hilltop.

name: Clayton Windmills
Wikipedia Extract: The Clayton Windmills, known locally as Jack and Jill, stand on the South Downs above the village of Clayton, West Sussex, England. They comprise a post mill and a tower mill, and the roundhouse of a former post mill.
why_interesting: Two beautifully restored windmills crowning the South Downs above Clayton.

name: Halnaker Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: Halnaker Windmill ( HAN-ə-kər) is a tower mill which stands on Halnaker Hill, north-east of Chichester, Sussex, England. The mill is reached by a public footpath from the north end of Halnaker, where a track follows the line of Stane Street before turning west to the hilltop.
why_interesting: A striking white windmill perched high on the South Downs near Chichester.

name: High Salvington Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: Durrington or High Salvington Windmill  is a Grade II listed post mill in High Salvington, Sussex that has been restored and is in full working order. The mill stands 320 feet (98 m) above sea level and is able to take advantage of incoming sea winds.
why_interesting: One of Britain's oldest working post mills, restored to full working order.

name: John Baker's Mill, Barnham
Wikipedia Extract: John Baker's Mill (or Barnham Windmill) is a grade II listed tower mill at Barnham, Sussex, England, which was under restoration and is now to be converted to residential use.
why_interesting: The restored remains of a traditional Sussex post mill.

name: Nutbourne Windmill
why_interesting: A picturesque post mill preserving West Sussex's agricultural heritage.

name: Wilton Windmill
why_interesting: One of Britain's finest working windmills, still producing flour today.

name: Auchinbaird Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: Auchinbaird Windmill or New Sauchie Windmill, was originally a late 17th or early 18th century vaulted tower grain windmill built into a low ridge located on the outskirts of the town of Sauchie, Clackmannanshire, Scotland. It was later converted into the Auchinbaird Dovecote or New Sauchie Dovecote, abandoned at an unknown date and later conserved as a landscape feature and visitor attraction.
why_interesting: The restored remains of a traditional Scottish estate windmill.

name: Ballantrae Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: The Ballantrae Windmill, on Mill Hill was a late 17th or early 18th century vaulted tower windmill, the ruins of which are located above the old raised beach cliffs on the outskirts of the village of Ballantrae in South Ayrshire, Scotland. Built around 1696 it was disused by 1799 and is a Category A Listed Building due to its important place in early industrial development.
why_interesting: The picturesque ruins of a coastal windmill overlooking the Firth of Clyde.

name: Dunbarney House Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: Dunbarney House Windmill is located just to the southwest of Dunbarney House near the Scottish town of Bridge of Earn, Perth and Kinross. A vaulted tower mill dating to the early 18th century, it is now a Category B listed building.
why_interesting: The restored remains of a historic Perthshire estate windmill.

name: Monkton Windmill
Wikipedia Extract: The Monkton Windmill, or Monkton Dovecote, was originally an early 18th century vaulted tower windmill located on the outskirts of the village of Monkton on the site of an Iron Age hillfort in South Ayrshire, Scotland. It was later converted into a dovecote and stood on the lands of the old Orangefield Estate.
why_interesting: The impressive remains of a traditional Ayrshire tower mill.

name: Aston Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Aston Hall is a Grade I listed Jacobean house in Aston, Birmingham, England, designed by John Thorpe and built between 1618 and 1635. It is a leading example of the Jacobean prodigy house.
why_interesting: One of Birmingham's finest Jacobean mansions, surrounded by beautiful parkland.

name: Barber Institute of Fine Arts
Wikipedia Extract: The Barber Institute of Fine Arts is an art gallery and concert hall in Birmingham, England. It is  situated in purpose-built premises on the campus of the University of Birmingham.
why_interesting: One of Britain's finest Art Deco galleries, home to an outstanding collection of European art.

name: Birmingham Town Hall
Wikipedia Extract: Birmingham Town Hall is a concert hall and venue for popular assemblies opened in 1834 and situated in Victoria Square, Birmingham, England. It is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: A magnificent Victorian concert hall celebrated for its grand architecture and world-class acoustics.

name: Bristol Old Vic
Wikipedia Extract: Bristol Old Vic is a British theatre company based at the Theatre Royal, Bristol. The present company was established in 1946 as an offshoot of the Old Vic in London.
why_interesting: The oldest continuously operating theatre in the English-speaking world.

name: Bristol Temple Meads railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Bristol Temple Meads is the oldest and largest railway station in Bristol, England. It is located 118 miles 31 chains (118.39 mi; 190.5 km) away from London Paddington.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most impressive Victorian railway stations, showcasing Brunel's engineering masterpiece.

name: Chester Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Chester Cathedral is a Church of England cathedral and the mother church of the Diocese of Chester. It is located in the city of Chester, Cheshire, England.
why_interesting: A former Benedictine abbey turned cathedral, with a medieval cloister at the heart of Chester's old city.

name: Derby Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: The Cathedral Church of All Saints, Derby, better known as Derby Cathedral, is a cathedral church in the city of Derby, England. In 1927, it was promoted from parish church status to that of a cathedral, creating a seat for the Bishop of Derby, which new Episcopal see was created in that year.
why_interesting: Home to a soaring 16th-century tower and the tomb of Bess of Hardwick, one of Elizabethan England's richest women.

name: Bluecoat Chambers
Wikipedia Extract: Built in 1716–17 as a charity school, Bluecoat Chambers in School Lane is the oldest surviving building in central Liverpool, England. Following the Liverpool Blue Coat School's move to another site in 1906, the building was rented from 1907 onwards by the Sandon Studios Society.
why_interesting: Liverpool's oldest surviving city-centre building, now home to independent shops, galleries and cafés.

name: All Souls College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: All Souls College (official name: The College of All Souls of the Faithful Departed, of Oxford) is a constituent college of the University of Oxford in England. Unique to All Souls, all of its members automatically become fellows (i.e., full members of the college's governing body).
why_interesting: One of Oxford's most prestigious colleges, famed for its magnificent library and Christopher Wren's sundial.

name: Ashmolean Museum
Wikipedia Extract: The Ashmolean Museum of Art and Archaeology () on Beaumont Street in Oxford, England, is Britain's first public museum. Its first building was erected in 1678–1683 to house the cabinet of curiosities that Elias Ashmole gave to the University of Oxford in 1677.
why_interesting: Britain's oldest public museum, housing treasures from ancient Egypt to contemporary art.

name: Balliol College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: Balliol College ( BAY-lee-əl) is a constituent college of the University of Oxford, England. Founded in 1263 by nobleman John I de Balliol, it has a claim to be the oldest college in Oxford and the English-speaking world.
why_interesting: One of Oxford's oldest colleges, educating leaders for more than 750 years.

name: Bodleian Library
Wikipedia Extract: The Bodleian Library () is the main research library of the University of Oxford. Founded in 1602 by Sir Thomas Bodley, it is one of the oldest libraries in Europe.
why_interesting: One of the world's greatest libraries, home to priceless manuscripts and literary treasures.

name: Brasenose College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: Brasenose College, formally The Principal and Scholars of the King's Hall and College of Brasenose in Oxford, or BNC, is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford in England. Founded in 1509 by Bishop of Lincoln William Smyth and Sir Richard Sutton, it traces its origins to an eponymous 13th-century medieval academic hall.
why_interesting: One of Oxford's most beautiful colleges, centred around an elegant medieval quadrangle.

name: Clarendon Building
Wikipedia Extract: The Clarendon Building is an early 18th-century neoclassical building of the University of Oxford. It is in Broad Street, Oxford, England, next to the Bodleian Library and the Sheldonian Theatre and near the centre of the city.
why_interesting: The grand neoclassical building that once housed Oxford University Press.

name: Corpus Christi College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: Corpus Christi College (formally, Corpus Christi College in the University of Oxford; informally abbreviated as Corpus or CCC) is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. It was founded in 1517 by Richard Foxe, Bishop of Winchester.
why_interesting: One of Oxford's smallest colleges, renowned for its medieval quadrangle and pelican sundial.

name: Exeter College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract:
Exeter College (in full: The Rector and Scholars of Exeter College in the University of Oxford) is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford in England, and the fourth-oldest college of the university.
The College was founded in 1314 by two brothers from Devon, Bishop Walter Stapledon and Sir Richard Stapledon, as an institution to educate clergy, and has been located on Turl Street since 1315.
why_interesting: One of Oxford's oldest colleges, founded in 1314 and centred on tranquil historic courtyards.

name: Pembroke College, Oxford
Wikipedia Extract: Pembroke College, a constituent college of the University of Oxford, is located on Pembroke Square, Oxford. The college was founded in 1624 by King James I of England and VI of Scotland, using in part the endowment of merchant Thomas Tesdale, and was named after William Herbert, 3rd Earl of Pembroke, Lord Chamberlain and then-Chancellor of the University.
why_interesting: A beautiful Oxford college with elegant Georgian architecture and picturesque gardens.

name: Eton College
Wikipedia Extract: Eton College (  EE-tən) is an English public school (a fee-charging boarding school) providing  education for boys aged 13–18, located in Eton, Berkshire. The school was founded in 1440 by Henry VI as Kynge's College of Our Ladye of Eton besyde Windesore, and is the largest boarding school in England.
why_interesting: One of the world's most famous schools, educating generations of Britain's leaders.

name: Boarstall Tower
Wikipedia Extract:
Boarstall Tower is a 14th-century moated gatehouse located in Boarstall, Buckinghamshire, England, and now, with its surrounding gardens, a National Trust property.
Until March 2020, the National Trust offered tours on Wednesday afternoons.
why_interesting: A remarkably preserved 14th-century fortified manor house surrounded by a medieval moat.

name: Belle Isle (Windermere)
Wikipedia Extract: Belle Isle is the largest of 18 islands on Windermere, a mere in the English Lake District, and the only one ever to have been inhabited. It is 1 km in length.
why_interesting: The largest island on Windermere, crowned by an elegant Georgian mansion.

name: Abbotsbury Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Abbotsbury Abbey, dedicated to Saint Peter, was a Benedictine monastery in the village of Abbotsbury in Dorset, England. The abbey was founded in the 11th century by King Cnut's thegn Orc and his wife Tola, who handsomely endowed the monastery with lands in the area.
why_interesting: The picturesque ruins of a Benedictine abbey overlooking the Dorset coast.

name: Canford School
Wikipedia Extract: Canford School is a public school (English fee-charging boarding and day school for pupils aged 13–18). Situated in 300 acres of parkland near to the market town of Wimborne Minster in Dorset, south west England, it is one of the largest schools by area.
why_interesting: A magnificent Gothic Revival school set within 250 acres of parkland.

name: Portland Castle
why_interesting: One of Henry VIII's finest coastal artillery forts overlooking Portland Harbour.

name: Beverley Minster
Wikipedia Extract: Beverley Minster, otherwise known as the Parish Church of Saint John and Saint Martin, in Beverley, East Riding of Yorkshire, is a parish church in the Church of England. It is one of the largest parish churches in the UK, larger than one-third of all English cathedrals and is regarded as a Gothic masterpiece.
why_interesting: One of England's greatest Gothic churches, celebrated for its soaring medieval architecture.

name: Hedingham Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Hedingham Castle, in the village of Castle Hedingham, Essex, is arguably the best preserved Norman keep in England. The castle fortifications and outbuildings were built around 1100, and the keep around 1140.
why_interesting: One of England's best-preserved Norman keeps, rising dramatically above the Essex countryside.

name: Bedales School
Wikipedia Extract: Bedales School is a coeducational boarding and day public school, in the village of Steep, near the market town of Petersfield in Hampshire, England. It was founded in 1893 by Amy Garrett Badley and John Haden Badley in reaction to the limitations of conventional Victorian schools and has been co-educational since 1898.
why_interesting: One of Britain's leading independent schools, set within a beautiful Hampshire estate.

name: Ashton Memorial
Wikipedia Extract: The Ashton Memorial is a folly in Williamson Park, Lancaster, Lancashire, England, built between 1907 and 1909 by the millionaire industrialist Lord Ashton in memory of his second wife, Jessy, at a cost of £87,000 (equivalent to £8.2 million in 2025).
why_interesting: Lancaster's iconic hilltop monument with panoramic views across Morecambe Bay.

name: Blackpool Tower
Wikipedia Extract: Blackpool Tower is a tourist attraction in Blackpool, Lancashire, England, which was opened to the public on 14 May 1894. When it opened, Blackpool Tower was the tallest man-made structure in the British Empire.
why_interesting: The iconic Victorian tower offering spectacular views across Blackpool's seafront.

name: Bolton Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Bolton Priory, whose full title is The Priory Church of St Mary and St Cuthbert, Bolton Abbey, is a Grade I listed parish church of the Church of England in the village of Bolton Abbey, within the Yorkshire Dales National Park in North Yorkshire, England. There has been continuous worship on the site since 1154, when a group of Augustinian canons moved from their original community in nearby village of Embsay and started construction of the present building, which is now situated within a scheduled monument under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act 1979.
why_interesting: The picturesque priory ruins beside the River Wharfe in the Yorkshire Dales.

name: Easby Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Easby Abbey, or the Abbey of St Agatha, is a ruined Premonstratensian abbey on the eastern bank of the River Swale on the outskirts of Richmond in the county of North Yorkshire, England. The site is privately owned but maintained by English Heritage and can be reached by a riverside walk from Richmond Castle.
why_interesting: The peaceful riverside ruins of a medieval Premonstratensian abbey.

name: South Cowton Castle
why_interesting: A remarkably complete 15th-century fortified manor house unlike any other in England.

name: Brinkburn Priory
Wikipedia Extract:
Brinkburn Priory is a former monastery built, starting in the 12th century, on a bend of the River Coquet, about 4 miles (6 km) east of Rothbury, Northumberland, England.
The priory church survived the dissolution of the monasteries because it was also a parish church.
why_interesting: The beautiful ruins of a medieval priory hidden within a wooded Northumberland valley.

name: Abingdon Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Abingdon Abbey (formally Abbey of Saint Mary) was a Benedictine monastery in Abingdon-on-Thames in the modern county of Oxfordshire in the United Kingdom. Situated near to the River Thames, it was founded in c.
why_interesting: The former site of one of England's greatest Benedictine abbeys.

name: Hexham Old Gaol
Wikipedia Extract: The Old Gaol, also known as the Manor Office, is a custodial building in Hallgate in Hexham, Northumberland, England. The building, which now operates as a museum, is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: England's oldest purpose-built prison, dating back more than 900 years.

name: Bessie Surtees House
Wikipedia Extract: Bessie Surtees House is the name of two merchants' houses on Newcastle's Sandhill, overlooking the River Tyne, that were built in the 16th and 17th centuries. Though commonly referred to solely as Bessie Surtees House, the property actually consists of three distinct properties; Bessie Surtees House, Milbank House, and Maddison House.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved 16th-century merchant's house overlooking the River Tyne.

name: High Level Bridge, River Tyne
Wikipedia Extract: The High Level Bridge is a road and railway bridge spanning the River Tyne between Newcastle upon Tyne and Gateshead in North East England. It was built by the Hawks family from 5,050 tons of iron.
why_interesting: The world's first road and rail bridge built on the same structure.

name: Bingley Five Rise Locks
Wikipedia Extract: Bingley Five-Rise Locks is a staircase lock on the Leeds and Liverpool Canal at Bingley (grid reference SE107399).  As the name implies, a boat passing through the lock is lifted or lowered in five stages.
why_interesting: The steepest staircase lock flight in Britain, lifting boats over 18 metres.

name: Chichester Cross
Wikipedia Extract: Chichester Cross is an elaborate Perpendicular market cross in the centre of the city of Chichester, West Sussex, standing 50 feet tall at the intersection of the four principal streets. It is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: The ornate medieval market cross at the heart of historic Chichester.

name: Crofton Pumping Station
Wikipedia Extract:
Crofton Pumping Station, near the village of Great Bedwyn in Wiltshire, England, supplies the summit pound of the Kennet and Avon Canal with water.
The steam-powered pumping station is preserved and operates on selected weekends.
why_interesting: The world's oldest working beam-engine pumping station, still steaming into life on special days.

name: Devizes Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Devizes Castle was a medieval fortification in the town of Devizes, Wiltshire, England, on a site now occupied by a Victorian-era castle. It is a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: The earthwork remains of a Norman castle overlooking the Vale of Pewsey.

name: Dundas Aqueduct
Wikipedia Extract: Dundas Aqueduct (grid reference ST785625) is an aqueduct in England which carries the Kennet and Avon Canal over the River Avon (the Somerset / Wiltshire border) and the Wessex Main Line railway. The aqueduct is near Monkton Combe, Somerset, and is about 2+1⁄2 miles (4 km) south-east of the city of Bath.
why_interesting: Thomas Telford's elegant cast-iron aqueduct carrying the Kennet and Avon Canal.

name: Marlborough College
Wikipedia Extract: Marlborough College is a public school (traditional description in the UK of elite fee-charging boarding schools) with day and boarding facilities for pupils aged 13 to 18 in Marlborough, Wiltshire, England. It was founded as Marlborough School in 1843 by the Dean of Manchester, George Hull Bowers, for the education of the sons of Church of England clergy.
why_interesting: One of Britain's leading independent schools, set within a historic Wiltshire estate.

name: Aberdeen railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Aberdeen railway station serves the city of Aberdeen in north east Scotland. It is the busiest railway station in Scotland north of the major cities of Edinburgh and Glasgow.
why_interesting: A magnificent Victorian railway station crowned by an impressive glass trainshed.

name: Craigston Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Craigston Castle is a 17th-century country house located about 4 miles (6.4 kilometres) north-east of Turriff, Aberdeenshire, Scotland, and is a historic home of the Urquhart family. The U-plan castle has two main wings flanking the entrance, connected by an elevated arch, and is surmounted by a richly corbelled parapet.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved Scottish baronial castle surrounded by landscaped parkland.

name: Crimonmogate
Wikipedia Extract: Crimonmogate is an estate near Crimond, Aberdeenshire. The estate formed part of Lonmay parish, dates back to the 14th century, and was included in the lands owned by the powerful Earls of Erroll.
why_interesting: A striking Greek Revival country house overlooking the Aberdeenshire countryside.

name: Duff House
Wikipedia Extract: Duff House is a Georgian estate house in Banff, Aberdeenshire, Scotland. Now in the care of Historic Environment Scotland, it is part of the National Galleries Scotland and is a Category A listed building.
why_interesting: A magnificent Palladian mansion housing one of Scotland's finest art collections.

name: Clachan Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Clachan Bridge (often, incorrectly, known as the Bridge over the Atlantic) is a simple, single-arched, hump-backed, masonry bridge spanning the Clachan Sound, 13 kilometres (8 mi) southwest of Oban in Argyll and Bute, west of Scotland. It links the west coast of the Scottish mainland to the island of Seil.
why_interesting: The charming 'Bridge over the Atlantic', linking Seil to the Scottish mainland.

name: Broughty Ferry railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Broughty Ferry railway station is a railway station serving the suburb of Broughty Ferry in Dundee, Scotland. It is sited 3 miles 38 chains (5.6 km) from the former Dundee East station, on the Dundee to Aberdeen line, between Dundee and Balmossie.
why_interesting: A handsome Victorian railway station overlooking the Tay Estuary.

name: Caird Hall
Wikipedia Extract: The Caird Hall is a concert auditorium located in Dundee, Scotland. It is a Category A listed building.
why_interesting: Dundee's grand concert hall and cultural landmark in the city centre.

name: Dudhope Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dudhope Castle is an extended late medieval tower house located on the southern face of Dundee Law in Dundee, Scotland.
why_interesting: A medieval castle transformed into one of Dundee's most recognisable landmarks.

name: Dundee Parish Church (St Mary's)
Wikipedia Extract: Dundee Parish Church (St Mary’s) is located in the east section of Dundee's "City Churches", the other being occupied by the Steeple Church. Both are congregations in the Church of Scotland, although with differing styles of worship.
why_interesting: Dundee's oldest surviving church, standing at the heart of the city for centuries.

name: Belhaven Brewery
Wikipedia Extract: Belhaven Brewery is a brewery based in Belhaven, Scotland. The brewery dates from 1719, at least; by 2005 it had become the largest and oldest surviving independent brewery in Scotland.
why_interesting: Scotland's oldest working brewery, producing beer since 1719.

name: Advocates Library
Wikipedia Extract: The Advocates Library, founded in 1682, is the law library of the Faculty of Advocates, in Edinburgh, Scotland. It served as the national deposit library of Scotland until 1925, at which time through an act of Parliament, the National Library of Scotland Act 1925 (15 & 16 Geo.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's finest legal libraries, housed within a magnificent historic building.

name: Barclay Viewforth Church
Wikipedia Extract: Barclay Viewforth Church is a parish church of the Church of Scotland in the Presbytery of Edinburgh and West Lothian.
why_interesting: A striking Gothic church designed by Frederick Thomas Pilkington.

name: Bute House
Wikipedia Extract: Bute House (Scottish Gaelic: Taigh Bhòid) is the official residence and workplace of the First Minister of Scotland. Located at 6 Charlotte Square in the New Town of Edinburgh, it is the central house on the north side of the square and was designed by Robert Adam.
why_interesting: The official residence of Scotland's First Minister on Charlotte Square.

name: Camera Obscura, Edinburgh
Wikipedia Extract: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions is a tourist attraction located in Outlook Tower on the Castlehill section of the Royal Mile close to Edinburgh Castle. The original attraction was founded by entrepreneur Maria Theresa Short in 1835 and was exhibited on Calton Hill.
why_interesting: Edinburgh's famous optical attraction with panoramic views from Castle Hill.

name: Canongate Kirk
Wikipedia Extract: The Kirk of the Canongate, or Canongate Kirk, serves the Parish of Canongate in Edinburgh's Old Town, in Scotland. It is a congregation of the Church of Scotland.
why_interesting: A beautiful 17th-century kirk closely linked to Scotland's royal history.

name: Dalmeny House
Wikipedia Extract: Dalmeny House (pronounced  dal-MEN-ee) is a Gothic revival mansion located in an estate close to Dalmeny on the Firth of Forth, in the north-west of Edinburgh, Scotland. It was designed by William Wilkins, and completed in 1817.
why_interesting: A magnificent Gothic Revival mansion overlooking the Firth of Forth.

name: Dean Cemetery
Wikipedia Extract: The Dean Cemetery is a historically important Victorian cemetery north of the Dean Village, west of Edinburgh city centre, in Scotland. It lies between Queensferry Road and the Water of Leith, bounded on its east side by Dean Path and on its west by the Dean Gallery.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most beautiful Victorian cemeteries, filled with remarkable monuments.

name: Edinburgh Academy
Wikipedia Extract: The Edinburgh Academy is a private day school in Edinburgh, Scotland, which was opened in 1824. The original building, on Henderson Row in Stockbridge, is now part of the Senior School.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's oldest independent schools overlooking Edinburgh's New Town.

name: Edinburgh College of Art
Wikipedia Extract:
The Edinburgh College of Art (ECA) is a department within the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland.
Tracing its history back to 1760, it provides higher education in art and design, architecture, history of art, and music disciplines for over three thousand students and is at the forefront of research and research-led teaching in the creative arts, humanities, and creative technologies.
why_interesting: One of Britain's leading art schools, producing generations of celebrated artists.

name: Edinburgh Waverley railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Edinburgh Waverley (also known simply as Edinburgh; Scottish Gaelic: Waverley Dhùn Èideann) is the principal railway station serving Edinburgh, Scotland. It is the second-busiest station in Scotland, after Glasgow Central.
why_interesting: Scotland's busiest railway station, framed by Edinburgh Castle and the Old Town.

name: Fettes College
Wikipedia Extract: Fettes College () is a co-educational private boarding and day school in Craigleith, Edinburgh, Scotland, with over two-thirds of its pupils in residence on campus. The school was originally a boarding school for boys only and became co-ed in 1983.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's most prestigious boarding schools, famed for its grand architecture.

name: Erskine Stewart Melville
Wikipedia Extract:
Erskine Stewart Melville (ESM) is an independent day school located in Edinburgh, Scotland managed by the Merchant Company of Edinburgh.  
The coeducational school was formed through the merger of all-girls' Mary Erskine School and the all-boys' Stewart's Melville College in 2026.
why_interesting: A distinguished Edinburgh school occupying an impressive Victorian campus.

name: Merchiston Castle School
Wikipedia Extract: Merchiston Castle School is an independent boarding school for boys in the suburb of Colinton in Edinburgh, Scotland.  It has around 470 pupils and is open to boys between the ages of 7 and 18 as either boarding or day pupils; it was modelled after English public schools.
why_interesting: A striking 15th-century castle that has served as a school for nearly 200 years.

name: Modern Two
Wikipedia Extract: Modern Two, formerly the Dean Gallery, in Edinburgh, is one of the two buildings housing the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art, one of Scotland's national art galleries. It is operated by National Galleries Scotland.
why_interesting: Scotland's outstanding collection of modern art housed in a grand neoclassical building.

name: National Library of Scotland
Wikipedia Extract: The National Library of Scotland (NLS; Scottish Gaelic: Leabharlann Nàiseanta na h-Alba; Scots: Naitional Leebrar o Scotland) is one of Scotland's National Collections. It is one of the largest libraries in the United Kingdom.
why_interesting: One of the world's great research libraries, preserving Scotland's written heritage.

name: National Monument of Scotland
Wikipedia Extract: The National Monument of Scotland, on Calton Hill in Edinburgh, is Scotland's national memorial to the Scottish soldiers and sailors who died fighting in the Napoleonic Wars. It was intended, according to the inscription, to be "A Memorial of the Past and Incentive to the Future Heroism of the Men of Scotland".
why_interesting: An unfinished national monument inspired by the Parthenon, commanding Edinburgh's skyline from Calton Hill.

name: Nelson Monument, Edinburgh
Wikipedia Extract: The Nelson Monument is a commemorative tower in honour of Vice Admiral Horatio Nelson, located in Edinburgh, Scotland.  It is situated on top of Calton Hill, and provides a dramatic termination to the vista along Princes Street from the west.
why_interesting: The iconic tower on Calton Hill offering panoramic views across Edinburgh and the Firth of Forth.

name: Dunmore Pineapple
Wikipedia Extract: The Dunmore Pineapple is a folly in Dunmore Park, near Airth in Stirlingshire, Scotland. In 1995, it was ranked "as the most bizarre building in Scotland".
why_interesting: Scotland's most eccentric folly, crowned by its famous giant stone pineapple.

name: Royal Scottish Academy Building
Wikipedia Extract: The Royal Scottish Academy building, the home of the Royal Scottish Academy, is an art museum in Edinburgh, Scotland. It is situated at the junction of The Mound and Princes Street in the centre of the city.
why_interesting: The grand neoclassical home of Scotland's national academy of art and architecture.

name: Culross Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Culross Abbey is a former Cistercian abbey in Culross, Scotland, headed by the Abbot or Commendator of Culross. Part of it is still used as the local parish church by the Church of Scotland.
why_interesting: The peaceful abbey at the heart of one of Scotland's best-preserved historic villages.

name: Anniesland Court
Wikipedia Extract: Anniesland Court is a 22-storey residential tower block in the Anniesland area of Glasgow, Scotland, designed by J Holmes & Partners and completed in 1968.  It is the tallest listed building in Scotland, and is remarkably similar to Ernő Goldfinger's later and more famous Trellick Tower in London.
why_interesting: A striking Brutalist apartment block recognised as one of Glasgow's architectural icons.

name: Burrell Collection
Wikipedia Extract: The Burrell Collection is a museum in Glasgow, Scotland, managed by Glasgow Museums. It houses the art collection of Sir William Burrell and Constance, Lady Burrell.
why_interesting: One of Britain's finest art collections, set within Pollok Country Park.

name: Glasgow Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract: Glasgow Cathedral (Scottish Gaelic: Cathair-eaglais Ghlaschu) is a parish church of the Church of Scotland in Glasgow, Scotland. It was the cathedral church  of the Archbishop of Glasgow, and the mother church of the Archdiocese of Glasgow and the province of Glasgow, from the 12th century until the Scottish Reformation in the 16th century.
why_interesting: Scotland's oldest mainland cathedral, famed for its magnificent medieval interior.

name: Glasgow Central railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Glasgow Central (Scottish Gaelic: Glaschu Mheadhain), usually referred to in Scotland as just Central or Central Station, is one of two principal main line rail terminals in Glasgow, Scotland. With 25 million passengers in 2024–2025, it is the seventeenth-busiest railway station in Britain and the busiest in Scotland, as well as the third-busiest station in the UK outside of London, behind Birmingham New Street and Manchester Piccadilly.
why_interesting: Glasgow's grand Victorian railway station, crowned by its vast arched roof.

name: Glasgow City Chambers
Wikipedia Extract: The City Chambers or Municipal Buildings in Glasgow, Scotland, has functioned as the headquarters of Glasgow City Council since 1996, and of preceding forms of municipal government in the city since 1889. It is located on the eastern side of the city's George Square.
why_interesting: One of Britain's most magnificent civic buildings, famed for its lavish marble interiors.

name: Glasgow Queen Street railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Glasgow Queen Street (Scottish Gaelic: Sràid na Banrighinn) is a passenger railway terminus serving the city of Glasgow, Scotland. It is the smaller of the city's two main line terminals; the larger is Glasgow Central.
why_interesting: A beautifully restored Victorian railway station beneath George Square.

name: Glasgow School of Art
Wikipedia Extract: The Glasgow School of Art (GSA; Scottish Gaelic: Sgoil-ealain Ghlaschu) is a higher education art school based in Glasgow, Scotland, offering undergraduate degrees, post-graduate awards (both taught and research-led), and PhDs in architecture, fine art, and design. These are all awarded by the University of Glasgow.
why_interesting: Charles Rennie Mackintosh's architectural masterpiece and one of Scotland's most influential buildings.

name: Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery
Wikipedia Extract: The Hunterian is a complex of museums located in and operated by the University of Glasgow in Glasgow, Scotland. It is the oldest museum in Scotland.
why_interesting: Scotland's oldest public museum, housing world-class art, science and natural history collections.

name: Aviemore railway station
Wikipedia Extract: Aviemore railway station serves the town and tourist resort of Aviemore in the Highlands of Scotland. The station, which is owned by Network Rail (NR) and managed by ScotRail, is on the Highland Main Line, 83 miles 31 chains (134.2 kilometres) from Perth, between Kingussie and Carrbridge, and is also the southern terminus of the Strathspey preserved railway.
why_interesting: The gateway to the Cairngorms, welcoming visitors to Scotland's mountain capital.

name: Annick Lodge and Greenville
Wikipedia Extract: Annick Lodge is an estate between Perceton and Cunninghamhead in North Ayrshire, Scotland.
why_interesting: A picturesque Georgian lodge overlooking the River Annick.

name: Barony of Ladyland
Wikipedia Extract: The Barony of Ladyland was in the old feudal Baillerie of Cunninghame, near Kilbirnie in what is now North Ayrshire, Scotland.
why_interesting: A historic Ayrshire estate with centuries of Scottish history.

name: Cathedral of The Isles
Wikipedia Extract: The Cathedral of the Isles and Collegiate Church of the Holy Spirit is a Category A listed cathedral of the Scottish Episcopal Church in the town of Millport on the Isle of Cumbrae. It is one of the two cathedrals of the Diocese of Argyll and the Isles, the other being St John's Cathedral in Oban.
why_interesting: Britain's smallest cathedral, set in the charming Victorian town of Millport.

name: Dr Gray's Hospital
Wikipedia Extract: Dr. Gray's Hospital is a district general hospital in Elgin, Moray, Scotland.
why_interesting: An elegant Georgian hospital designed by Alexander Reid.

name: Kelburn Castle
why_interesting: A colourful fairytale castle famous for its hand-painted murals and woodland estate.

name: Erskine Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Erskine Bridge is a multi span cable-stayed box girder bridge spanning the River Clyde in west central Scotland. The bridge connects West Dunbartonshire with Renfrewshire and can be used by all types of motor vehicles, cyclists and pedestrians.
why_interesting: A striking cable-stayed bridge spanning the River Clyde.

name: India of Inchinnan
Wikipedia Extract: India of Inchinnan is now a commercial site in Inchinnan, Renfrewshire, Scotland, that was formerly used for various industrial uses.  It includes the former office block of India Tyres of Inchinnan - a Category A listed building in the art deco style, designed in 1930 by Thomas Wallis of Wallis, Gilbert and Partners.
why_interesting: The spectacular Art Deco headquarters built for India's jute empire.

name: Bemersyde House
Wikipedia Extract:
Bemersyde House is a historic house in Roxburghshire, Scotland.

The nearest towns are Newtown St.
why_interesting: One of Scotland's oldest continuously inhabited houses overlooking the River Tweed.

name: Alloway Auld Kirk
Wikipedia Extract: The Alloway Auld Kirk, which dates back to the 16th century, is a church ruin  in Alloway, South Ayrshire, Scotland, celebrated as the scene of the witches' dance in the poem "Tam o' Shanter" by Robert Burns.
why_interesting: The atmospheric ruins of Robert Burns' family church beside the Brig o' Doon.

name: Brownsbank
Wikipedia Extract:
Brownsbank (Brounsbank in Scots) is a cottage close to the small settlement of Candymill to the north of Biggar in Scotland.
It is best known as  the former home of the poet Hugh MacDiarmid.
why_interesting: The former home of poet Hugh MacDiarmid overlooking the Clyde Valley.

name: David Livingstone Birthplace Museum
Wikipedia Extract: The David Livingstone Birthplace Museum is a biographical museum in Blantyre, South Lanarkshire, Scotland, dedicated to the life and work of the explorer and missionary David Livingstone. The museum is operated by the David Livingstone Trust and is housed in a category A listed building often referred to as Shuttle Row.
why_interesting: The birthplace of David Livingstone, celebrating the explorer's remarkable life.

name: Dunblane Cathedral
Wikipedia Extract:
Dunblane Cathedral is a Church of Scotland church in Dunblane, Scotland. 
The lower half of the tower is pre-Romanesque from the 11th century, and was originally free-standing, with an upper part added in the 15th century.
why_interesting: A magnificent medieval cathedral with one of Scotland's finest surviving Gothic interiors.

name: St Michael's Parish Church, Linlithgow
Wikipedia Extract: St Michael's Parish Church, Linlithgow,  is one of the largest burgh churches in the Church of Scotland. In 2024, it united with St Ninian's Craigmailen (also in Linlithgow), Torphichen Kirk and Avonbridge Church to create the new Linlithgow and Avon Valley Church.
why_interesting: The historic church beside Linlithgow Palace, crowned by its distinctive stone spire.

name: Conwy Railway Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Conwy Railway Bridge carries the North Wales coast railway line across the River Conwy between Llandudno Junction and the town of Conwy. The wrought iron tubular bridge, which is now Grade I listed, was built in the 19th century.
why_interesting: Robert Stephenson's masterpiece carrying trains across the Conwy Estuary.

name: Menai Suspension Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Menai Suspension Bridge (Welsh: Pont y Borth or Pont Grog y Borth) is a suspension bridge spanning the Menai Strait between the island of Anglesey and the mainland of Wales. Designed by Thomas Telford and completed in 1826, it was one of the world's first major suspension bridges, and second such bridge designed to carry vehicular traffic, after the Union Chain Bridge (1820) across the River Tweed.
why_interesting: Thomas Telford's world-famous suspension bridge spanning the Menai Strait.

name: Monnow Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: Monnow Bridge (Welsh: Pont Trefynwy Welsh pronunciation: [pɔnt tre:vənʊɨ]), in Monmouth, Wales, is the only remaining fortified river bridge in Great Britain with its gate tower standing on the bridge. Such bridge towers were common across Europe from medieval times, but many were destroyed due to urban expansion, diminishing defensive requirements and the increasing demands of traffic and trade.
why_interesting: Britain's only remaining medieval fortified river bridge.

name: Newport Transporter Bridge
Wikipedia Extract: The Newport Transporter Bridge (Welsh: Pont Gludo Casnewydd) is a transporter bridge that crosses the River Usk in Newport, South East Wales. The bridge is the lowest crossing on the river.
why_interesting: One of the world's last working transporter bridges, spanning the River Usk.

name: Pont Fawr
Wikipedia Extract: Pont Fawr (also known as Llanrwst Bridge) crosses the River Conwy in the town of Llanrwst, Conwy County Borough, Wales. Traditionally attributed to the architect Inigo Jones, it was built in around 1636.
why_interesting: The iconic medieval bridge at the heart of Llanrwst.

name: Church of St Mary the Virgin, Llanfair Kilgeddin
Wikipedia Extract: St Mary the Virgin is the former parish church for Llanfair Kilgeddin, near Usk in Monmouthshire, south east Wales.  It is a Grade I listed building, notable for its significant Arts and Crafts interior.
why_interesting: A beautifully preserved medieval church overlooking the Usk Valley.

name: Church of St Nicholas, Trellech
Wikipedia Extract: The Church of St Nicholas, Trellech, Monmouthshire is a parish church with its origins in the 14th century. The historical and architectural evidence suggests that it was constructed largely in a single building period c.1300.
why_interesting: A medieval church standing beside one of Wales' largest village greens.

name: Penallt Old Church
Wikipedia Extract: Penallt Old Church is located just outside the village of Penallt, Monmouthshire, Wales.  It is a Grade I listed building as of 19 November 1953.
why_interesting: A peaceful medieval church with sweeping views across the Wye Valley.

name: St Bridget's Church, Skenfrith
Wikipedia Extract: The Church of St Bridget (or St Bride) lies at the north end of the village of Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, Wales.  It is an active parish church and a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: A picturesque medieval church beside the River Monnow.

name: City Hall, Cardiff
Wikipedia Extract: City Hall (Welsh: Neuadd y ddinas) is a municipal building in Cardiff, Wales, UK. It serves as Cardiff's centre of local government. It was built as part of the Cathays Park civic centre development and opened in October 1906.
why_interesting: Cardiff's magnificent Edwardian civic centrepiece, crowned by its clock tower.

name: Cymer Abbey
Wikipedia Extract: Cymer Abbey (Welsh: Abaty Cymer) is a ruined Cistercian abbey near the village of Llanelltyd, just north of Dolgellau, Gwynedd, in north-west Wales, United Kingdom.
why_interesting: The tranquil ruins of a 12th-century Cistercian abbey in southern Eryri.

name: Dinefwr Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Dinefwr Castle (Welsh: Castell Dinefwr; also known as Old Dynevor Castle) is a ruined castle overlooking the River Towy near the town of Llandeilo, Carmarthenshire, Wales. It lies on a ridge on the northern bank of the Towy, with a steep drop of one hundred feet to the river.
why_interesting: A spectacular Norman castle overlooking the Tywi Valley within a beautiful National Trust estate.

name: Gladstone's Library
Wikipedia Extract:
Gladstone's Library, known until 2010 as St Deiniol's Library (Welsh: Llyfrgell Deiniol Sant), is a residential library in Hawarden, Flintshire, Wales, UK. 
Gladstone's Library is Britain's only Prime Ministerial Library and serves as the national memorial to William Ewart Gladstone. It is home to a large collection of printed items and archives that reflects Gladstone's main interests in history, literature, theology, and politics.
why_interesting: Britain's only residential library, welcoming visitors to stay among thousands of books.

name: Abbey of St Mary, St Dogmaels
Wikipedia Extract:
The Abbey of St Mary (also known as St Dogmaels Abbey) is Grade I listed ruined abbey in St Dogmaels in Pembrokeshire, Wales, on the banks of the River Teifi and close to Cardigan and Poppit Sands.
It is the ruins of a medieval abbey, originally founded in 1115 by the Fitzmartin family of Cemais.
why_interesting: Atmospheric medieval ruins made for exploring.

name: Clytha Castle
Wikipedia Extract: Clytha Castle (Welsh: Castell Cleidda) is a folly near Clytha between Llanarth and Raglan in Monmouthshire, south east Wales.  Dating from 1790, the castle was built by William Jones, owner of the Clytha Park estate as a memorial to his wife, Elizabeth, who died in 1787.
why_interesting: A striking castle with history, drama and a real sense of occasion.

name: Haverfordwest Priory
Wikipedia Extract: Haverfordwest Priory (Welsh: Priordy Hwlffordd) was a house of Augustinian Canons Regular on the banks of the Western Cleddau at Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, Wales.
why_interesting: A beautiful medieval abbey with real atmosphere and history.

name: Blaenavon Ironworks
Wikipedia Extract: Blaenavon Ironworks (Welsh: Gwaith Haearn Blaenafon), officially spelled Blaenafon Ironworks since 2024, is a former industrial site which is now a museum in Blaenavon (Welsh: Blaenafon), Wales. The ironworks was of crucial importance in the development of the ability to use cheap, low quality, high sulphur iron ores worldwide.
why_interesting: A historic building with character, history and plenty of reasons to visit.

name: Cadoxton Court Dovecote
Wikipedia Extract: Cadoxton Court Dovecote is a medieval structure in Cadoxton, in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. Dating from the 13th century, it is the largest of the remaining medieval dovecotes in the Vale and a Grade I listed building.
why_interesting: One of the largest historic buildings in Britain, with plenty of character.

name: Castle Farmhouse, St Georges-super-Ely
Wikipedia Extract: Castle Farmhouse is a medieval farmhouse in St Georges super Ely, in the Vale of Glamorgan, south Wales. Its origins are as part of the Norman castle of the Le Flemings, after which it declined in status, first to a manor house, and subsequently to a farmstead.
why_interesting: A medieval castle that still feels every bit the stronghold.

name: Coedarhydyglyn
Wikipedia Extract: Coedarhydyglyn or Coedriglan, formerly Old Coedarhydyglyn (meaning 'the wood along the glen'), is a private Grade I listed neo-classical regency villa and estate on the western rim of Cardiff, less than half a mile from Culverhouse Cross, southeast Wales. It is accessed via the A48 road between Cardiff and St.
why_interesting: A historic house with plenty of character and a setting worth the trip.

name: Great Western Colliery
Wikipedia Extract: Great Western Colliery, which included the shaft known as the Hetty Pit, was a coal mine located at Hopkinstown, near Pontypridd, Glamorgan in South Wales. Operating from 1851 to 1983, the mine was the site of a major disaster in 1893 that killed 63 miners.
why_interesting: A historic building with character, history and plenty of reasons to visit.
